speechtext: ['Hear, hear!']

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is my unhappy duty to announce to the House that our friend and colleague the former member from London East, Jim Jepson, died in London an hour ago. There will be tributes on Monday. I know that hon. members would want to have the weekend to consider the announcement and make the appropriate remarks, as is the custom in this place.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday in the House in a non-answer to a question I raised with the Minister of State for Forests about job losses because of the lack of signed forest agreements, the minister said he was not aware of any problems. The minister had only to consult his own department's information to see that 43 silvicultural workers in New Brunswick have lost their jobs because of the lack of a forest agreement.
In British Columbia, the staff of Forestry Canada are approaching members of our caucus expressing concern about their jobs because of the confusion caused by the government's lack of action. Worse is that the trained staff in Forestry Canada have the skills that are needed in a renewed forest agreement. We cannot lose them.
The minister is obviously not aware of the concern in the forest community about these unsigned agreements. He should sign them now.

Mr. Speaker, on November 18, I visited the community of Mistissini, where I observed the deplorable condition of 141 homes built according to the standards of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development when the former Liberal government was in power.
Today, these homes are very unsanitary and have been condemned by the Department of Health. Nevertheless, these government-built slums, with no electricity, water or plumbing, still house nine families because other accommodation is lacking.
On many occasions Chief Henry Mianscum has demanded that these outdated, unhealthy, dangerous shacks be replaced.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat again that our Government must correct the errors of this department; otherwise, that community would be entitled to CIDA programs in the same way as the Third World.

Mr. Speaker, in 1990 the Army, Navy and Air Force veterans in Canada will commemorate their 150th anniversary. It is the oldest veterans' organization in the country. The group's earliest members fought in the war of 1812.
Throughout its long history, the members of ANAF served their country with distinction. In recognition of its proud tradition, the ANAF last year asked Canada Post to issue a commemorative stamp in 1990. Just last month, the veterans learned, to their shock, that Canada Post had refused the request for a commemorative stamp. This is an insult to our veterans who sacrificed so much for our country. Surely they deserve more than the cursory rejection they received from Canada Post in light

of the contribution they have made to ensure our freedom.
I urge the government to reconsider this offensive snub to Canada's oldest veterans organization. I strongly urge the government to issue a stamp commemorating the 150th anniversary of ANAF.

Mr. Speaker, as the process of reform continues in eastern Europe, parliamentarians must remain aware of difficulties in other areas of the world, particularly the continuing problem of family reunification for Ethiopian Jews. Although some 17,000 Ethiopian Jews were airlifted to Israel in 1984-85,12,000 to 15,000 are still separated from their families in Ethiopia.
The United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights of which Ethiopia is a co-signatory, obliges nations to permit and assist in the reunification of families separated by migration. Given the Canadian people's generous assistance in aiding Ethiopia and the current downsizing of Soviet aid, Canada is in a strong position to exercise leadership on this vital human rights issue. Almost 1,500 Ethiopian Jewish children remain separated from their families, an injustice entering its fifth year.
I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to place this issue high on the agenda in our relations with Ethiopia.

Mr. Speaker, since nine Haitians who were to be deported yesterday did not go to Mirabel (Airport) and it is becoming increasingly obvious that the reign of terror continues in Haiti under President Avril, I ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration and the Conservative government to go back on their decision
concerning the moratorium and to stop all planned expulsions immediately.
I make this request for all those poor people who fear persecution in Haiti, in particular, for Gertrude Nazaire and her daughter Minerve and for Lucienne Oscar, her husband and two children, who made representations at my riding office in Montreal.
I do not understand why the minister does not use her discretionary powers and take humanitarian action, as requested by the Montreal Rights and Freedoms League, among others.
What game is the Conservative Party playing with the Montreal Haitian community?
Last week, the Conservative ministers from Montreal undertook to ask their immigration colleague to change her position. However, the minister's secretary told the press that they made no such request. This hypocrisy is unacceptable. The inhuman deportations must stop right now.

Mr. Speaker, this week marks the sixtieth anniversary of the Bowater Mersey Paper Company Ltd. Established by Isaac Walton Killam in 1929, Bowater Mersey has become the economic backbone of Queens County, Nova Scotia employing some 800 people directly and another 2,100 indirectly.
Under the leadership of general manager Harold Dobson and his predecessors, Bowater Mersey is a model of corporate commitment to the community and a company that values its employees and sees their interests as important as those of the company.
This year Bowater Mersey is completing a $150 million modernization that will not only improve the efficiency of the plant but enable it to meet the highest environmental standards, ensuring that Bowater Mersey will continue to be internationally competitive for years to come.
Congratulations to the Bowater Mersey Paper Company and all associated with it.

subtopic: MONTREAL SOUTHWEST COMMITTEE ON ECONOMIC RECOVERY AND EMPLOYMENT
MONTREAL SOUTHWEST COMMITTEE ON ECONOMIC RECOVERY AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week, the Montreal southwest committee on economic recovery and employment released a major report on the economic and social development of our region.
The report's main recommendations are to create a community development corporation that would co-ordinate the activities of all parties and to invest $200 million, part of which would be new money, over a three-year period.
In Montreal, the southwest region has a very high unemployment and welfare rate. Forty per cent of the population lives below the poverty line.
The government has chosen to ignore the many instances of plants closing down.

The situation in Montreal southwest is serious. The committee's report is very well done. It should be acted upon immediately.

The government should now show that it means business and indicate right away that it intends to give these recommendations its unqualified support. People are tired of waiting.

Mr. Speaker, it is symbolic and sad that there are currently reports of sexual abuse of children from each end of our country. From Vancouver we heard that a judge has incredibly commented that a three year old girl shares responsibility in a sexual abuse case against a 33 year old man. In St. John's, Newfoundland it was just announced that Mount Cashel orphanage will be closed. We all know why.
I call on the Solicitor General and the Attorney General to do all in their power to protect children from sexual abuse through strong legislation and strong law enforcement. I call on all Canadians to protect children
in any way possible and report any sexual abuse to authorities.
Today's children and youth have many hurdles and challenges that we adults have placed in their way. They do not need this one and every effort must be made to eradicate sexual abuse of children from Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the federal government claims to support sustainable development. The Prime Minister signs declarations abroad to this end. The Minister of the Environment bravely promises action. But when it comes to the crunch, as with the closing of the B.C. fisheries because of pollution, we hear a different story.
The Minister of Fisheries says the government is not prepared to prosecute pulp and paper companies discharging toxins into coastal waters. He uses the pathetic excuse that the minute quantities of toxins contained in the effluents are difficult to measure, even though the accumulation in fish can be measured. His logic defies logic.
Should we expect more from this government which has an abysmal record in prosecuting polluters? It gives the Department of the Environment less than 1 per cent of the federal budget and does not ratify the law of the sea. Either this government does not mean what it says or it does not understand what sustainable development means.

Mr. Speaker, most Canadians were delighted last June when this House passed legislation providing that the pensions of widows and veterans would continue to be received until their death.
Prior to this bill, if a widow who had been receiving a pension as a result of her husband's death was to remarry, she would lose that pension. All parties supported this bill that was to provide up to a total of $28 million annually in pensions to approximately 4,500 widows and widowers. Unfortunately, to date, of those eligible only 700 have applied. The reality is that there has not been much of an effort to locate these people.

November 29, 1989
The Minister of Veterans Affairs says that they simply do not have the budget to extensively advertise this legislative change.
If this government has the funds to take out full-page ads in every major newspaper across the country promoting the Conservative position on the GST bill before it is even tabled in the House, then surely it can increase the Veterans Affairs budget to allow for a similar ad to be placed to reach these worth while Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, today we heard the news that the well-known Romanian gymnast, Nadia Comaneci, had to flee her country because she prefers to live in freedom outside her native country instead of under the repressive regime of Nico-lae Ceausescu. I think it is sad that even those who are privileged under the system are no longer satisfied with their life in Romania.
Not long ago, I met a number of my constituents who reminded me of the suffering of the Romanian people: severe economic hardship as a result of misguided economic policies, a total lack of freedom and human rights, and repression of national and religious minorities. Canadians hope they will soon see the following changes in Romania: free elections, respect for human rights and a complete renewal of the government, leading to the return of genuine democracy.
I appreciate the fact that the Secretary of State for External Affairs issued a press release on November 24, condemning the treatment of Mr. Mazilu by the Romanian authorities, and that Canada's ambassador to the United Nations raised the same issue that day. I strongly urge the government to renew its efforts to help improve the situation in Romania.

Mr. Speaker, young athletes would be horrified if their parents suggested that they take anabolic steroids. Yet
parents may be giving their children daily fixes of a far more harmful hormone. Vitamin D, routinely added to milk, baby food and breakfast cereal has been found to be one of the most potent steroid hormones available, and a very toxic food additive.
Scientists at Simon Fraser University say people should be avoiding it unless there is a clear medical reason for its use. Vitamin D has been found to increase aging in vital organs such as arteries, kidneys and bones leading to cardiovascular disease and osteoporosis. The vitamin may also increase the body's retention of toxic metals such as lead, cadmium and aluminum, a suspected culprit in Alzheimer's disease.
Federal regulations require its addition to milk, margarine and infant formula and may be responsible for unintentional infant poisonings. The Minister of National Health and Welfare should undertake a detailed study of the health risks of vitamin D in the interests of Canadians who because of government regulation may be exposing themselves to excessive levels of consumption.

Mr. Speaker, the World Health Organization has designated December 1 as World AIDS Day. The Ontario provincial government is commemorating the day by giving substantial financial support to four clinics for AIDS victims and to the University of Toronto for research. The federal government should commemorate AIDS Day by acting on the recommendations of the report on AIDS commissioned by the Minister of Health last June and released recently.
The report calls on the government to establish a new agency to oversee an increased fight against AIDS; to establish appropriate mechanisms for surveillance, prevention and control; as well, to address and eliminate high risk behaviour; and to help develop a vaccine for prevention as well as treatment modalities to control the disease and to ensure that the human rights of those affected are respected and their families and care givers receive adequate support.
November 29, 1989

I urge the government to accelerate the development of a national strategy on HIV infection and AIDS and make a commitment now to spend more time and money combating this most serious global disease.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. JAMES F. COOKE

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. JAMES F. COOKE
speechtext:
I wish to advise hon. members that Mr. James Cooke, Deputy Principal Clerk in the Journals Branch is retiring today after 35 years of combined service to the Government of Canada and to the House of Commons.
Mr. Cooke began his career at the House in 1963 in the Index and Reference Branch and from there moved on to the Journals Branch where he has served in the position of Deputy Principal Clerk since 1975.1 am sure the House will want to join with me in wishing him all the very best in his retirement and our very great thanks for his years of service to all of us.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MR. JAMES F. COOKE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Right Hon. John N. "Rimer (Leader of the Opposition):
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. In his absence I will put it to the Deputy Prime Minister. All the senior citizen groups in this country and an overwhelming number of the social service agencies, including the government's own National Advisory Council on Welfare, stated that the Conservative proposal to claw back seniors' pensions and family allowances is an attack on the universality of our social programs. It is also an attack so far as our pensioners are concerned on what they consider to be a right of citizenship in this country.
Yesterday, the Conservative members on the parliamentary committee set up to study that clawback rammed through a vote to hear only four witnesses on this tremendously important income tax change. The Minister of Finance will not even appear personally before the committee to give it an explanation. I cannot remember in my parliamentary career where an income
Oral Questions
tax change of this importance has been done by stifling the witnesses in this country who want to appear before the committee.
Can the Deputy Prime Minister tell us why the government is afraid to let senior citizens appear before the parliamentary committee to give their views on this grossly unfair change to the income tax, the clawback of senior citizens' pensions?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the Hon. Leader of the Opposition that it was with great pleasure that I appeared in front of the committee and answered all the questions that were put to me during that period.
Mr. "Rimer (Vancouver Quadra): One hour.

The hon. member must be aware that this government has been faced over the last year with a major problem, which is largely of his making, and that no part of government spending can be left out.
As far as the Old Age Security benefits are concerned, I would like to state that during the pre-budget consultation representatives of various groups came to us, a member of One Voice for example, and said: " We agree with the economic council that people with over $50,000 of income should have their OAS taxed back". These benefits are, of course, important. Universality has been protected. Every Canadian entitled to it will receive his or her cheque. They were taxed before and they will continue to be so that the lower income people are well protected.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance should have appeared personally before the committee. The Minister of State excused himself after one hour, in order to listen to the Prime Minister's speech on abortion. That is all very well. But he should appear again before the committee, this time with his Minister of Finance, and allow witnesses across the country to testify before the commitee. That is the problem.

I will again direct my question to the Deputy Prime Minister. Just as with the goods and services tax, the Minister of Finance maintains that on this issue of the clawback of the senior citizens' pensions, he is right and everybody else in the country is wrong.

Oral Questions
I will say to the Deputy Prime Minister, a man who appreciates Parliament, I guess the Conservatives are coming to a point where democracy is becoming a bit of a nuisance to them and they want to cut off some of this debate.
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!

Why will the government not at least put into the legislation a guarantee that the clawback on senior citizens' pensions will be indexed against inflation. Given the government's track record, given the personal record of the Minister of Finance, why should senior citizens, or anyone else, trust the minister? Why should anyone trust his word that he will review the situation in a few years. If the government is serious, put that indexation clause in the legislation.

I was in the position to indicate to the committee yesterday-and I would remind the right hon. Leader of the Opposition that it is for the committee to set its agenda, and not for me-that this government will stand on its record.
Look at the various programs we have set and reviewed every year in a positive manner. We have said repeatedly that for the old age security benefits, we would do the same every year.

Mr. Speaker, my next question is directed to the Minister of State (Seniors). I wonder why the Minister is getting a cabinet minister's salary and has such a large staff, considering the circumstances. If the minister is supposed to represent Canada's seniors, why has she failed to defend their cause in Cabinet? Since all senior citizens' groups in this country are opposed to the pension clawback for seniors, why didn't the minister insist on letting these groups appear before the parliamentary committee? She is supposed to speak for our seniors but they have no voice before the comittee. I suggest that the minister immediately ask the Deputy
Prime Minister or the Prime Minister to intervene so that her Tory colleagues will let Canada's senior citizens' groups express their views before the committee.
speakername: Right Hon. John N. Dimer@Leader of the Opposition

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I repeat that it is up to the committee to decide how it intends to proceed. However, I can give this House and Canada's seniors the assurance that I am the Minister who defends their interests in Cabinet. Whenever a government project, initiative or program is proposed, we make sure that the rights and benefits of Canada's seniors are protected. We have maintained the universality of our programs. We intend to improve our social programs, and what we are now asking 4 per cent of Canada's seniors to do is to help us reduce the deficit so that we will have the flexibility we need to improve our social programs.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice who I believe is in the Chamber. It involves the remarks made by a county court judge in British Columbia that a three-year old girl, herself sexually assaulted, was sexually aggressive.
Has the minister used his specific power under Section 63 of the Judges Act to require the Judicial Council of Canada to commence an inquiry immediately into this horrific situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am aware of the case in question. I have to tell my hon. friend that the case is presently under appeal. Until the appeal period is over and all court actions are finished, I think it would be inappropriate to take any action or to comment on it in this place.

Mr. Speaker, all Canadians stand appalled at this situation. If the minister has not and will not use his Section 63 authority, can he tell this House what is being done to ensure that attitudes such as this do not continue to be voiced in Canadian courts?
November 29, 1989

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, any comment that I might make in response to that could be taken as affecting the case in question. While I sympathize with the point of view of my hon. friend in a general way, I point out to her that it is a matter of public record that a complaint is being made to the Canadian Judicial Council. I am sure if that is the case and it follows through, the council will address itself to the complaint received.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister who is no doubt aware of the existence of Conservative Party documents which outline a strategy of linking government contracts, grants or policies to corporate donations.
In at least the case of the Royal Bank in 1987, the targeted hit was made by the PC Canada Fund chairman, David Angus, a close friend of the Prime Minister. He succeeded in a $40,000 hit when an earlier bagman had failed.
Since political favours for cash leads to the corruption of democratic institutions, will the Deputy Prime Minister take steps to amend Canada's election laws to ensure that such activity is made illegal?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that what is important is that issues of this matter be properly conducted in accordance with the Elections Act.
I think the hon. member is referring to an internal document or memo that has never really been put in place. It is the substance of a story that goes back to November 19 and November 20, 1986. It is interesting to note that Broadcast News Toronto indicated that it did not want any further use of the story because it was outdated and is really old news that is being rehashed.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Justice. Perhaps the Minister of Justice can clarify this for those corporations
Oral Questions
which may have felt that they were put under a similar kind of pressure to that of the Royal Bank.
Will the minister tell Canadians, Canadian businesses and members of this Chamber whether the soliciting of donations from donors by reminding them of government business they have received is illegal or is in his view just improper?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what is important is that under the Elections Act there is full public disclosure of contributions received, whether from individuals, corporations or unions. As long as this is conducted in compliance with the provisions of that act, that is the most important element. If the hon member has any evidence to the effect that there is a violation of that act, then he should take appropriate action.

Mr. Speaker, what we are talking about here is signals between government and big business. Canadians are skeptical about the benefits of the donation connection between big business and the Tories.
Does the Deputy Prime Minister really expect Canadians to believe that there is no connection between the $660 million aviation radar contract awarded to Hughes Aircraft Company and the wink-wink, nudge-nudge, you-know-what-I-mean promise of Hughes to locate in the ridings of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and the Minister of Science and Technology or-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the Chair has been patient, but the hon. member is straying into an area where he ought not to be. The minister may want to respond. I certainly will not call upon him to do that if he does not want to.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member talks about signals. If he has any evidence of signals, let him take the appropriate action.
If the hon. member wants to open up the bidding process, let him do that. There is an appropriate place for that to be done in committee or he can raise it specifically on the floor of the House of Commons.
My understanding is that the procedures were closely followed. If he has something against a contract being awarded to British Columbia, Alberta and western Canada, Ontario and other parts of the country, but specifically a good portion of it going to his home province and to the province of Alberta, let him say so

November 29, 1989
Oral Questions
and not hide behind that sort of silhouette of purity that he sometimes suggests but does not always purvey.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Deputy Prime Minister. Is it the practice of the government to provide to any political party and specifically to the PC Canada fund lists of government contracts awarded and, if so, will he make these lists available to all members of this House?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is referring to a story which was discredited three or four years ago. I am sure that even when he was not in the House he was probably aware of that. This is a stoiy that has been rehashed and the memo that the hon. member refers to has never been adopted.

Mr. Speaker, I note the Deputy Prime Minister did not answer my question. I asked if he would make the lists available, not whether the story was discredited. I will go on with a supplementary question.
The government has established a commission to study the means by which political parties are funded. Will the Deputy Prime Minister instruct his bagmen to appear before this commission and reveal their practices and their lists?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad that there was one positive element in that particular question, the fact that there is a commission that was established to study the elections procedure, the fund-raising activities. This issue has been debated in the House and outside the House. I hope if the hon. member wants to make reference to the commission about who should appear or who should not appear, he can make that representation directly to the commission.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Last week the Deputy Prime Minister and the Solicitor General, both in response to questions in this House, refused to release the contents of the November 7 Peter White letter relative to the RCMP conduct of the Richard Grise affair. This morning those contents were
leaked by RCMP sources through the press. That leak process, after refusal to release it here, is contemptuous to the members of this House and demands to be called such.
Will the Prime Minister, now that the contents of the letter are on the street, immediately release the contents of the letter from his office and put an end to the speculation about the letter's purpose?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Solicitor General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is nothing new in what I saw this morning, except that some information seems to have appeared in the press. The situation has not changed since last week, which means we still have a case before the courts in connection with the document that was discussed last week. I believe it was the RCMP's decision not to release it. It was not the government's. This document is part of an RCMP investigation on the situation. And since the case is already before the courts, I think it would be inappropriate for us to release it. If it ever is released, the RCMP will decide to do so, not the government.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Solicitor General. I have to remind him that RCMP sources are quoted in the article of this morning.
The public has real concern over possible politicization of the RCMP by this government and there are many public questions which are going unanswered. Now, as if to confirm the suspicion that there really does exist a political faction inside the RCMP, we have this perfectly timed leak this morning to take the pressure off the government.
When will the Solicitor General take action to locate this suspected political connection and stop the erosion of public confidence in the RCMP, and what will those steps be?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the best way to stop, as the hon. member said, the erosion of confidence in the RCMP would be to stop asking questions and levelling accusations or making allegations against the RCMP.
November 29, 1989

I will repeat, as I have said many times, that we must respect the work being done by the RCMP in the course of its investigation. I believe the RCMP Commissioner has already answered all these questions and will appear before the Justice Committee as soon as he is back from Interpol, within the next few days.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to return to the work of the legislative committee on the clawback bill. I must say I was surprised at the comments that I heard earlier from the government benches. Surely Canadians who are concerned about the cuts in VIA Rail should be happy to know that there is still a railroad running in Canada. It is called the legislative committee on Bill C-28.
My question to the Deputy Prime Minister on this important issue of government policy is this: the government in Bill C-28 is doing one of two things, it is either ending universality or it is introducing a discriminatory tax based on age and family size. Now, which is it?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to give the hon. member information that I did not have when I last rose in this House. The committee apparently has asked the clerk to invite some of the groups which asked to be heard. Therefore, that should at least-
Only four.

Well, a little while ago it was none.
I would also like to remind the hon. member that this measure was introduced in the budget some months ago and has been debated and discussed on many occasions. It was also discussed in this House in the debate on the budget. It will be discussed again in committee and will come back to the House.
Therefore, I remind the hon. member that the threat to our social programs, and this one in particular which is extremely important to our seniors, does not come from any measure that we take on this side, but from the growing deficit and from the debt we inherited. We
Oral Questions
should be concerned that next year we will be paying interest in the range of $40 billion. This is something that has to be tackled and no program of this government can escape scrutiny. So this is my answer.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to hear that the minister sounds like he wants to invite more groups to the committee but the record will show that he did not answer the question.
[Translation\
Since the pension and family allowance clawback constitutes the most sweeping change in Canada's social policy in 20 years, is the Deputy Prime Minister prepared to inform the House that the Minister of Finance will appear before the Committee to answer questions about this tax which discriminates against seniors and families?

Mr. Speaker, I repeat, this is not a discriminatory tax. A number of seniors receive additional benefits, and in line with our general program review, these measures must apply to all programs.
I think we should also remember that, for instance, when the system is fully operational, only 50,000 people on high incomes will have to pay back all part of their benefits; 74,000 will pay a part: in all, 130,000 seniors out of three million will be partially affected by these measures.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister, I have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister.
During last year's federal election, the Prime Minister met in Edmonton with the Lubicon Band Chief, Bernard Ominayak, ostensibly to get negotiations back on track after 50 years of on-again but mostly off-again attempts to reach a settlement.
In January, the government presented its formal offer, which even Premier Getty tells us is "deficient", declaring the Lubicons could take it or leave it, and any consideration of compensation would have to go to court.
With the Lubicon people shutting down Crown-owned oil and gas operations on their traditional lands and with

November 29, 1989
Oral Questions
federal officials meeting on this matter with Alberta officials in Calgary tomorrow and Friday, will the government direct its officials to make clear, and announce, the government's willingness now to resume negotiations with the Lubicon on all aspects of their claim, including a compensation package?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, ever since we made this offer last January, we have been prepared to go back to the table to discuss the fair and comprehensive offer that was made to the Lubicons. Unfortunately, the Lubicons have been refusing to come back to the table.

Will the minister not agree that what he calls a fair offer is a pastiche of things that the band might do. It in no way comes close to dealing with the question of compensation. In fact, government negotiators ruled out compensation in their September 8 letter: "On the question of compensation, we invite the band to pursue this claim in the Canadian courts". Will he agree that in fact he is willing to negotiate nothing? Agreeing to that, will he now announce that the government has changed its policy and will negotiate?

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the government has not changed its policy but is prepared to negotiate, has been prepared to go back to the table and is still prepared to go back to the table. It has directed the negotiators to meet with the provincial-
Listen to the Lubicon.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Perhaps I can be permitted to answer, since a valid question has been put.
We have directed our negotiators to speak with the provincial negotiators because the Lubicons have voiced concerns to the provincial negotiators about our offer, but not to us. We are analysing those concerns. We are prepared to go back to the table and discuss those concerns and address them in an offer that is comparable to any other claim settlement that has been made in Canada since.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade.
On November 21, Quebec farmers demonstrated on Parliament Hill, and after talking to farmers from Abitibi, I want our joint programs, marketing boards and quotas to be protected 100 per cent.
My question is as follows: Could the Minister confirm in the House today that Quebec farmers will not be ignored or abandoned by his department, more specifically in connection with GATT Article 11, and that the Quebec government will have its say in the talks?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to assure the hon. member that neither the farmers of Quebec nor the farmers of Canada will be forgotten by the government at any time, whether it is in the MTN negotiations or otherwise.
With respect to those negotiations, I made it clear to the Cairns Group when I was in Bangkok last week dealing with a comprehensive agriculture proposal what Canada's position is in the matter of supply-management boards. I explained to them that we did not think the new GATT Article 11 would be subject to tariffication with reference to those new rules and how they worked. In other words, the Mazankowski-Blais position was put clearly to the Cairns Group and put clearly to the world on behalf of the Quebec farmers.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Last week in the native community of Kingfisher Lake, located in northwestern Ontario, a 16-year-old boy took his life. This is the fourth suicide in that community of 300 in the past two years.
There have been 40 suicides in six communities in the Shibogama Tribal Council area in the past two and a half years. The suicide rate in native communities located in northwestern Ontario is seven times the national average.
My question to the minister is this: Will the minister request immediately a judicial inquiry into the increasing suicides in northwestern Ontario with a view to finding solutions to this very disturbing crisis in the native communities?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. gentleman raising this very serious question. The whole issue of suicide, particularly suicide among Canada's native peoples, is of particular concern to me.
The department is commissioning studies to be done on issues related to suicide to get a better understanding of the reasons for it, particularly among young Canadians. Additionally, we have programs in place that are designed to help with native problems on reserves and to try to deal particularly with problems related to alcoholism and drug abuse.
The success in cutting the suicide rates in a number of instances has been quite good. For example, I had the privilege recently of visiting one reserve in western
Oral Questions
Canada, outside of Edmonton, where there was a significant improvement in terms of reduction of the suicide rate. We will continue to do everything we can to be helpful in terms of assisting in that.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the same minister. The minister did not listen to my question. Obviously he and the government are not listening. It has been two and a half years since we brought this particular situation to the attention of this government. There have been 40 suicides in these small areas of northwestern Ontario, with a population of only 1,800. It is time that we act and not just listen.
My supplementary question relates to the 21 aboriginal communities in my riding in which there are only three mental health workers. That is what I am talking about when I talk about the fact that there is nothing being done. There are only three mental health workers in a large geographic area to try to discuss those matters of interest to the people of those communities.

Any input the hon. gentleman wants to make in terms of suggestions I would be glad to receive from him. But I can tell him that the department puts a high priority on the improvement of services in native communities, it puts a high priority on consultations with native groups and certainly we are taking whatever measures that we can to try to ensure that the problem of suicide among Canada's native peoples is dealt with. He thought it was an important step forward, that there was an agreement that the foreign minister of the Soviet Union and I would meet to discuss actions we might take in the Arctic.

important step forward in the relations between Canada and the Soviet Union, and also important in terms of the possibility of making progress on our joint concerns and interests in the Arctic.

Mr. Speaker, there may have been progress, but in terms of demilitarization there is no response to the initiative offered by the President of the Soviet Union in his Murmansk speech some time ago. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again the hon. member is dead wrong. The Murmansk proposal was made by Mr. Gorbachev in 1987.1 responded to it in the fall of 1987. We then wrote the Soviet Union asking for specific proposals that they might make. We received none.
When Mr. Gorbachev and the Prime Minister of Canada met in Moscow a week ago, the Prime Minister of Canada said: "We are interested in the Murmansk proposal. What specifically are you proposing? Is there anything you want us to follow up?" Mr. Gorbachev said then: "We think it would be very valuable for Mr. Shevardnadze and the Canadian foreign minister to meet to pursue issues that Canada might propose or that the Soviet Union might propose". That is substantial progress by any fair judgment.
Members of the Liberal party should recognize that this trip has allowed Canada to make very substantial steps forward including in terms of establishing progress and agreed regimes in the Arctic. Instead of seeking every occasion to make narrow, partisan attacks, they should recognize a national accomplishment.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to amend the Canada Elections Act to require the government to call a by-election within a stated time from the issue of the Speaker's warrant when a vacancy occurs in this chamber.
The purpose of the bill is to ensure that the by-election is held promptly-I believe 80 days is provided from the date of issue of the warrant-so that the government cannot sit around as it has done for the last six months and do nothing while the people of Chambly are deprived of representation in the House.

That this House condemns the government for its insensitivity to the tremendous difficulties being faced by Canada's farmers and other rural Canadians which are the direct result of the government's failure to respond adequately to the pressing and specific needs of Canadian farmers in financial, trade, marketing and other areas, which are creating a dangerous level of anger and frustration, as was seen in the recent massive demonstration by thousands of farmers on Parliament Hill; and further, that the government be condemned for not supporting producer-controlled marketing agencies and boards.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have this motion before the House today because it was exactly a week ago yesterday that we saw the largest farm protest rally on Parliament Hill in a decade.
The motion tries to express the feelings of those thousands and thousands of farmers from Ontario and

Quebec who are extremely concerned with where the government is going with its trade policies, with its income support policies and with its farm programs.
We only have to look at the press clippings from last Wednesday, exactly a week ago, to see the incredible concern that is expressed. I look at a clipping from The Toronto Star which reads, "Quit harming agriculture Tories told". It shows a picture of effigies of the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister which were subsequently burned on the lawns of Parliament. It points out the views of the president of the Quebec farmers, the UPA group, who stated that the government is bargaining away farm support schemes and subsidies in international trade.
The article goes on to state, "Farmers say the government is adopting an American view at General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade talks by calling for the removal of agricultural market controls." It goes on to state, "As a kite depicting an American eagle clutching a pig hovered over his head," the Deputy Prime Minister spoke.
That protest rally is just the tip of the iceberg. Farm groups across the country feel betrayed, especially in light of the policies which the government has adopted in the past year.
You will recall that during the free trade debate the Prime Minister was interviewed by The Wall Street Journal on April 3, 1987. Fie said, "U.S. trade remedy laws cannot apply to Canada, period".
He went on to say in that same interview, "You can't have a free trade arrangement and expect the traditional laws of countervail to apply".
Those words spoken by the Prime Minister were echoed as well by the Minister for International Trade in July of 1987 when he spoke at the St. John's Board of Trade meeting. He said, "Unless we get out from under the threat of countervail and other U.S. trade remedy laws and unless there is an effective dispute settlement resolution to bind the Americans to their commitments, a free trade agreement with the United States would not be a good deal for Canada".
That is the kind of commitment which farmers felt had been made on their behalf. Of course, no such commitment was made. We only have to look at the Canadian pork producers who have had imposed since early September a countervail of 3.6 cents a pound, or eight cents a kilo, on pork coming from Canada.
Supply
The distressing part is that it was not imposed because of some pre-existing law, it was imposed because the Americans changed the law after they signed the free trade deal, after they implemented the legislation for the free trade deal. They immediately passed an amendment to their countervail law which enabled them to launch a countervail duty case against pork, as had been done with hogs for the past year and a half.
Surely everybody, even the people on this side of the House, thought that when we signed the free trade deal, we were in a free trade area and that there was going to be some good will, an understanding that there would be less adversarial kind of activity. Yet Congress passed legislation to extend the countervail duty law.
I think people were concerned that the government did not appeal it. It did not go to the GATT when those amendments to the countervail duty law were passed over a year ago. So we have a situation now where beyond the countervail duty which applies to pork, which has been in place since about 1985, we have a new countervail on hogs. However, we expect that within the next year, in March sometime, there will be a review of the subsidy levels in Canada. The tripartite hog stabilization program has been singled out, and countervail duty on pork which is 3.6 cents a pound now may well become 11 cents or 12 cents a pound later. We had a situation where the pork processing plants in this country said, "Look, if we are going to have a retroactive countervail imposed on us of that magnitude, we are going to stop sending pork to the United States". The Canadian Pork Council had to take the initiative of imposing a $2 per hog levy for every hog marketed in this country, whether it is consumed in Canada, or whether it is consumed in Japan or other importing countries from Canada.
In effect, the only way that we are going to get access to the U.S. market that the Prime Minister promised he would deliver-for the 25 per cent or so of Canadian hogs that go to the United States-is to impose a levy of $2 on every hog sold in the country. That is what it costs under the FTA, or the CUSTA, which is the new name. I think the government was just so embarrassed by having something called an FTA, a free trade agreement, that it changed it to Canada-U.S. Trade Agreement. Obviously, if pork producers in this country have to buy access by paying $2 for every hog marketed, it does not sound very free to them. That is one of the tremendous concerns which has been expressed by the UPA, by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture and by the representatives

Supply
from New Brunswick who were here a week ago yesterday.
Just as important was the concern expressed by the UPA and the OFA in regard to the situation of the dairy industry. A year ago last January the Minister of Agriculture said that there was no problem with the tariff being reduced under the free trade deal for processed agriculture products, such as yoghurt and ice-cream, because he was going to put them over on to the import control list. I think most farmers in the country believed that there was some security in what he was doing, but in fact there was none.
It is obvious now and it was pretty obvious at the time that there was no agreement with the Americans to accept that kind of an import control on yoghurt and ice cream. Immediately those import controls were imposed in late December of last year the United States Government demanded a GATT panel. That panel reviewed the situation and struck down the placing of import controls on yoghurt and ice-cream, as well as a half dozen other novelty dairy products.
This is perhaps the most damaging part of the whole free trade fiasco, as I would call it. The government has not accepted the decision by the GATT panel, but I am sure if the Deputy Prime Minister wanted to be totally honest he would admit that within a week the government will accept it but perhaps not implement it for a year. That decision states that import controls under Article 11 of the GATT can only be applied to raw, unprocessed agriculture commodities such as milk. That decision, to me, means that if the kind of import controls we are talking about can be placed on milk, they can be placed on 2 per cent milk, on chocolate milk and perhaps even buttermilk, something that can be drunk, but not on something like yoghurt, ice-cream, cheese, butter or skim milk powder which are processed products.
That is the kind of thing that drives the OFA, the Ontario Milk Marketing Board, the UPA-every supply management producer in this country-wild. Because if it applies only to yoghurt and ice-cream, then it applies to all these other commodities. In the dairy industry we
are talking about 60 per cent of our production, that is all the industrially produced processed milk.
Clearly, the government deceived Canadian farmers when it said that their supply management systems were protected. The minister says we want to negotiate a better description of Article 11, and I am sure that he does. I do not know of any Canadian who is interested in supply management in the agriculture industry who does not. But I think we should look back at those negotiations because it was not as if this decision by the GATT panel came out of the air in September. It was a deliberate decision by the United States. This comes back to the whole question of whether there is any goodwill in the free trade deal. I maintain there is not any. You have to look across the whole range of products, but as far as I can see there has been no great outpouring of such in agriculture or in other commodities for trade.
The Government of Canada through the Department of Agriculture negotiated all summer trying to get the Americans to accept a larger quota. I think our quota was set at something like 340 tonnes or so. The government offered to go to around to 1,000 or 1,500, but the Americans were not buying. Clearly, that is not going to be a decision that will be easily overturned.
I have a copy of a speech that was given just today by the Ontario Minister of Agriculture and Food who was speaking to the Ontario Federation of Agriculture. He has just returned from meetings with the United States minister of agriculture, the Secretary of Agriculture and the Secretary for Trade. In his speech to the Ontario Federation of Agriculture in Toronto today he said that according to Ambassador Hills every internal domestic program has to be on the table. They object to any system that restricts a market, and at present they see U.S. farmers as having no opportunity to put their milk into Ontario.
He went on to say that the Americans are determined to aggressively access our market. The Milk Industry Foundation is particularly unabashed in stating that they want our market.
Clearly, from the negotiations that went on last summer, the United States is absolutely determined that it will have full access to the Canadian market. Clearly,
November 29, 1989

no provision was made for this in the free trade deal, and the results will be devastating for our supply management. What applies to the dairy industry could well apply to the poultry industry as well.
Those are two of the major concerns which the 10,000 or 12,000 farmers from across Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick were expressing to members of Parliament and to the government a week ago yesterday.
Another great concern is that we are part of two trading groups negotiating at the GATT. One is our Canada-U.S. CUSTA free trade group. Unfortunately, as I have already said, they do not agree with our position. They want to have full access. They want to get rid of our supply-management system. They have always been open about that, but it was up to our government in negotiating the CUSTA agreement to ensure that.
The second group of which we are a part is the Cairns group. Clearly from the statements made by the Australians and some others in the Cairns Group they likewise are opposed to our position. How strong can our position be? I will not say that there are no supporting countries, because I hope some of the Scandinavian and some of the European countries will support us in the GATT to strengthen our position with regard to Article 11, and hopefully to recover what has been lost in the GATT panel decision.
We have to be especially concerned when the two trading groups that we are going to the GATT with, the Americans and the Cairns Group, are opposed to our position. One sometimes wonders whether the position that the minister puts here in the House of Commons is exactly the position that he is putting in the Cairns Group, or that the Minister for International Trade or our negotiators are putting.
An article in the October 27 edition of The Globe and Mail quoted a federal agricultural trade official who stated, when talking about the GATT negotiations, that the division in the agricultural community over supply-management has caused Canadian negotiators to adopt a Jekyll and Hyde approach at the multilateral trade negotiations.
Supply
As the Australians say, we speak with a forked tongue on these issues. When officials in the Department of Agriculture are saying that, we tend to become nervous. We like what the minister is saying here, that he wants to maintain supply management, but we are concerned with the position he has been put in, not only by the free trade deal which did not secure the import control side, but because of the removal of the tariffs our whole food processing industry is putting great pressure on our supply management system as well.
Those are two very important issues that the thousands and thousands of farmers on the lawns of Parliament were concerned with.
The third issue which is very important is the fact that the government is making dramatic cut-backs in its farm support programs. The minister talks about the billions and billions of dollars, but what the farmers are concerned about is the $500 million that he cut back last spring. There is no western grain stabilization payment. There is no special grains program.
Clearly, the government did not make adequate provision in the free trade deal for marketing boards. They are in the greatest jeopardy they have ever felt. Pork producers are being saddled with a $2 fee just to buy access to the U.S. market. Our support programs are being unilaterally dismantled, while some time during the next five or six years we supposedly will be negotiating a subsidy code. Our Durum wheat producers are being threatened with a countervail.
Never in my memory has the viability of Canadian agriculture been so threatened as it has been this past year by the government's actions and lack of action.

speechtext: On questions and comments, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank our critic on agriculture for leading off this debate with some very insightful comments on Canadian farming.
I was wondering if I could ask him a question dealing with some particular problems in the west. As he knows full well, because of his research and his consultations throughout the Canadian agricultural community, there has been a tremendous amount of debt created by the current policies of this government.

November 29, 1989
Supply
The Minister of Agriculture is very fond of coming to us and telling us how much more money he is spending each year in the west. He never tells us the number of farmers who are going broke and increasing debt load.
For example, there has been a 48 per cent increase in foreclosures in Manitoba in the last seven months. That comes before the tough season, the November to May season when farmers really get into a lot of difficulty. There are 108 foreclosures that have been initiated in the last few weeks in Manitoba alone. This sort of activity is what makes the Manitoba farmer so insecure under the present regime.
We have a minister responsible for the Wheat Board in our province and a Minister of Agriculture from the west. They seem to have walked away from the problems in our region and do not respond to the farmers when they are going through this debt crisis. It is anticipated that this is just the beginning and that Manitoba is headed for a very, very trying year.
I wonder if our critic could respond and comment as to whether or not there is any hope under the present policy. Is there any hope under the new policy given to us by the Minister of Agriculture a few weeks ago and can we expect the farmers to receive any more help? I am not very optimistic, and I was wondering if he is.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the question from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. It is impossible to say what the government is going to do. It is capable of doing anything, as I outlined in my earlier remarks. Clearly the direction seems to be, if you read the document "Freedom to Grow" or "Growing Together" or freedom to go, as some people call it, that the whole mood is toward reducing government expenditures.
If you look at the budget of the Minister of Finance last spring, the only comment with regard to the Farm Credit Corporation was to remove the commodity-based mortgage which did provide some concessional funding.
The agriculture committee of the House of Commons did a major report in the spring of 1988. It put forward a number of innovative and worth-while suggestions about directions we might take to improve the farm debt situation. In the Speech from the Throne, in the budget, in the Minister's statement, there was no mention or
specific proposal with regard to how the government might provide new and innovative arrangements.
Many other programs were cut, and there were about seven or eight in the budget. For example, the advance payment which we fought very hard to save provided farmers with very worth-while cash flow assistance, perhaps only for three or four months, or in some cases for six months or a year, but it provided interest-free cash advances which were very important. That is going to cause very great pressure this winter. I do not think the farm debt crisis is over. The report of the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities states that the number of farms that have been taken over by municipalities or are being attached by municipalities is growing at an alarming rate.
Garth Stevenson, president of the Saskatchewan Pool, states that farmers are going to require assistance in the magnitude of $500 million before cropping time next spring. Clearly there is financial assistance needed. It is being cut back unilaterally, even though our American counterparts are continuing their new farm bill. All reports say that it is going to be as generous and supportive as the 1985 farm bill. Yet, we are cutting back many programs on a unilateral basis.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Algoma for bringing forth this motion. While I do not agree with it, it does provide an opportunity to outline some of the things this government has done for agriculture, the tremendous record of support that this government has had with respect to agriculture and also to outline some of the things that we propose to do in the future, a new vision and some new directions.
I am disappointed that the hon. member did not propose anything new. It is basically the same old litany of gloom and doom and a repetition of what we have heard before. He ignores in his comments the reality of trade laws, the reality of GATT rules, the reality of what the free trade agreement really is and that trade remedies apply equally to all participating countries.
We get the impression that the Liberals are still fighting the last election. They attempt to strike fear and anxiety into the hearts and minds of the producers. Every problem that arises with respect to agriculture is blamed on the free trade agreement. That reminds me of the
November 29, 1989

statement that was made by the former finance critic, the hon. member for Etobicoke North, I believe, when he said something to the effect that every sparrow that falls is going to be blamed on the Canada-U.S. trade agreement.
The hon. member also said that we are part of two negotiating groups, the Canada-U.S. negotiating group and the Cairns Group. I do not know where he got that nonsense. We are part of the Cairns Group and we certainly support many of the objectives of the Cairns Group because it does provide us with an opportunity to deal with the debilitating situation that has affected our export-oriented agriculture industry. But we have carved out our own position and that was clearly outlined in a comment made by the Australian trade minister, Mr. Duffy, when he told local journalists that Canada's insistence on maintaining protection for its dairy industry could be a problem in reaching a final consensus.
As we heard from the Minister for International Trade today, Canada has staked out a very clear position with respect to Article 11, with respect to supply-management systems and the fact that we intend to pursue this issue in an attempt to clarify and strengthen Article 11, something which the hon. members opposite forbid us to do. They have suggested not touching Article 11 because we are going to tamper with it. Now they are saying that we have to do something about it. That has always been our position, to clarify and strengthen, because we foresaw some of the difficulties that came down with respect to the ice cream and yoghurt decision.
The motion condemns the government for its insensitivity to the difficulties facing Canada's farmers. I will be the first one to acknowledge that there are problems in the agriculture industry. There always have been problems in the agriculture industry and there probably always will be in some area or another. I will acknowledge the difficulties that the grain and oilseed sector has gone through with depressed prices as a result of the trade war between the United States and the European community with its common agricultural policy, the United States with its Export Enhancement Program, and of course Canada was caught in the cross-fire. We saw incomes drop from an average of $2.4 billion in
Supply
market receipts in that period 1981-84 to a low of $475 million in 1987, which is a drop of about 75 per cent.
It was for that reason that the Prime Minister provided the leadership in bringing this issue before the GATT. We could not withstand this debilitating exercise that was destroying our farmers and also placing a very heavy burden on the federal treasury. It was because of the Prime Minister's leadership that we were able to raise the agriculture issue to the top of the agenda at the GATT proceedings. That is really, in the final analysis, the only long-term solution to this very serious problem.
We have to recognize that 50 per cent of our agriculture receipts come from the export market. We must restore order in the international market-place if our industry is going to survive. That is very fundamental and very basic, and hon. members opposite tend to forget that.
In this particular case, because of the debilitating impact that the trade war had upon the grains and oilseeds sector, we did respond. We responded in an unprecedented fashion. I will get into that a little later.
We also had a drought situation that was as serious or perhaps more serious, and statistics will bear me out on this, as it was during the dirty thirties in terms of precipitation and in terms of the extent of heat. Over the last four-year period, as recorded at our stations in Swift Current and in Lethbridge, precipitation was less and the intensity of the heat was greater. We have also had other disasters. In other areas we have had floods. In other areas we have had grasshoppers. You name it, and they have been afflicted with it. On each and every one of these occasions this government has responded.
With respect to the drought in 1988-1989, a $850 million program was initiated with some sharing from the provinces. Most of the cheques have been mailed out. Some are still in the process of being mailed out. There are still some appeals left to be settled. It is very difficult to design these programs to ensure that there is fairness and equity right across the board. I challenge hon. members opposite to consider that. We tried to devise a program in consultation with the agriculture community with representatives of the various farm organizations, and it is not as easy as one would like. There are always areas of unfairness and discrimination and inequities. That is why we want to try to bring about

November 29, 1989
Supply
substantive change to our crop insurance programs and our safety net programs so that we can better deal in a more fair and equitable manner with these.
In 1984 and 1985 there was $200 million provided for drought. In 1988, $100 million for drought.
The hon. member across the way mentioned the Special Canadian Grains Program, $2.1 billion was paid out in lieu of the trade war to try to meet that gap, that deficiency between what we considered to be a fair market value, as compared to what the producers received in the grains and oilseeds sector, $2.1 billion. In addition to that, some $300 million in losses were covered in the Canadian Wheat Board account.
Under the Western Grain Stabilization program, some $4 billion was paid out over 1985-1989, and the vast majority of that money was provided for by the federal government. There were record payments under the Agricultural Stabilization Program. With respect to crop insurance, about $200 million annually is paid by the federal government. The Crop Re-insurance program has cost the federal government something in the order of $700 million over the last three or four years.
In addition, there were special Farm Credit Corporation programs such as moratoriums, shared risk mortgages, and other initiatives and innovative programs to reduce interest rates. During this period of time in the last four or five years we have had some of the lowest rates we have had in five years.
We injected $600 million of new equity into the Farm Credit Program. In other words, we transferred debt into equity. We came forth with a rural transition program. We established Farm Debt Review Boards. I must say this has been a very successful initiative, because for something in the order of 77 to 80 per cent of the people who came before the Farm Debt Review Boards, while there have been difficulties in this particular area, there have been satisfactory arrangements made to provide ways and means where they may stay on the farm and maintain farming as a lifestyle. There have been over 10,000 applications under this program; some $360 million has been provided. Basically, through practical common sense, we have been able to bring the creditors
and the farmer together in such a way that they have been able to sort out their difficulties.
Farm credit arrears have been reduced by about 50 per cent. Fuel price relief was provided at $200 million per year. Under the Western Grain Transportation Act, freight rate relief was provided. We provided a stabilization program for red meats and additional livestock feed assistance for the Atlantic region was provided.
We provided help for the tobacco farmers. Some $62 million has been committed for that program. We provided help for the apple growers, a $6 million stabilization fund, and initiated a countervail against the cheap imports coming in from the United States. We provided help for the grape growers in terms of their adjustment, a $128 million program. We provided help for the sour cherry industry, again another countervail action by Canada.
We helped the onion sector, again another countervail action by Canada. We provided assistance to the potato industry, again another countervail action against cheap imports coming into the country. We provided help for the com producers, again through the actions of a countervail. We are providing help for the pork producers, both in terms of fighting a countervail action and in terms of providing food relief in the form of pork products to Poland.
There have been agri-food subagreements signed with literally every province. There may be one or two that are still in the final stages of negotiation, but basically there have been programs in place and programs renewed.
The federal-provincial soil conservation programs have been signed with most of the provinces. There may be one or two that are still remaining. When that is completed, that will constitute a $150 million joint shared program.
We provided assistance to the honey producers. We provided assistance to the white bean producers. We have helped the dairy producers in their price adjustments. We are defending their interests at the GATT. We established a long-term five-year dairy policy, something that the Liberals never thought of, never dreamed of. They left the dairy farmers hanging in thin air from

year to year. Again, we established a dairy task force to help deal with all the problems that exist with regard to trade negotiations and pricing, et cetera.
We defended the beef producers against subsidized imports from the European Community. Again, with respect to the poultry industry, we are establishing a task force so that they can take full advantage in exploiting the market opportunities and adjusting their production patterns to ensure that that industry can grow.
There have been industries that have gone through painful adjustments such as the tobacco industry, the grape industry, the honey industry and the Canola producing industry.
However, Mr. Speaker, this so-called insensitive government provided unprecedented support for agriculture since it has been in office. If you look at the Public Accounts of Canada you will find that very clear between the years 1984-85 and 1987-88. In the 1984-85 fiscal year, $3,224.8 million; 1985-86, $3,210.1 million; 1986-87, $4,501.9 million; 1987-88, $6,124.4 million; 1988-89, $4.6 billion, a total of $21,700 million, well in excess of $4 billion a year, compared to about $2 billion under the previous administration.
If we look at the grain and oilseeds industry, we find that in the period 1981-84 the federal government of the day provided about $350 million in support. In that period, 1984-85 to 1988-89, some $11.7 billion, almost $12 billion, has been provided, or an average of $2.3 billion per year, as compared to $350 million per year under the Liberals.
That is what this insensitive government has done. This insensitive government has provided major increases in net farm income. Under the Liberals, net farm income averaged $3.7 billion annually between the period 1981-84. Under our government, farm income reached $5.2 billion in 1988 on the basis of preliminary statistics. That average between 1985 and 1988 is $4.5 billion. That is a 25 per cent increase over the period 1981 and 1984 when the Liberals were in office.
Under the Liberals, the agriculture industry was stagnant. It was depressed. It was despondent. There was human misery. The industry was troubled, but no one listened, no one cared. Farm bankruptcies, to answer my hon. friend from Winnipeg, achieved an all-time high in 1984 of 551 bankruptcies.

The year you took over.

speechtext:
Yes, that is the mess we took over then, as we took over the mess of debt that we inherited from the Liberal party as well.
Farm bankruptcies have been reduced by some 50 per cent. Projected bankruptcies are at a level of 240 this year, still too high.
However, Mr. Speaker, the 551 bankruptcies were simply the tip of the iceberg because there were many other farmers who voluntarily left the farm or were foreclosed. It does not tell the whole story about the human misery that that government and party inflicted upon the farmers: 23 per cent and 24 per cent interest rates; 13 per cent and 14 per cent inflation; land values soared, and when they dropped there was a problem. Money was easy to get, and 97 per cent of the people who found themselves in financial difficulty traced their problems right back to that period.
It is the same thing that the Liberals did when the leader of their party said: "Why should I sell your wheat?". Well, we provided leadership to the Canadian Wheat Board. Wheat sales increased from 17 per cent to 22 per cent. It is slipping somewhat because of the drought situation, but nonetheless we demonstrated that we were interested in selling farmers' wheat.
In the livestock industry, receipts have been up by about 10 per cent. Exports are up from $620 million in 1981 to $1 billion in 1988. It is interesting to note that while these people across the way badmouth the Americans, 95 per cent of our exports of cattle go to the United States, and 93 per cent of our fresh and frozen beef and veal exports go to the United States of America. We have taken our agriculture trade balance from $2.8 billion in 1985 to $4 billion in 1988.
There are many more opportunities. The bilateral trade agreement provides many opportunities in Ontario, western Canada and in Quebec. I will quote a couple of headlines: "Fruitbelt Reaps FTA Profit". We know as well that in terms of the vegetable industry, there is an expectation that the demand for vegetables shipped to the United States will increase by some 80 per cent.
The Ontario wine producers: "Woo Upscale New York Citizens. Roll over Bordeaux and California, the Niagara region of Ontario is breaking into the New York wine
