market". This clearly establishes that they can compete with the best in the world.
Here is another headline from the Calgary Herald. "Huge U.S. Market Offers Big Gains". In an article from the World of Beef in September, a Bank of Montreal senior economist says: "The FTA is the best assurance we can get against sideswiped protectionism". It goes on to say that the market-driven economies of most industrialized countries position Canada very well in terms of taking advantage of new trading opportunities. Food processing investment is up by 15 per cent over the previous year. With the GST, that situation will improve further still.
The hon. member for Algoma quoted the Minister of Agriculture for the province of Ontario. I was interested in noting as well, as reported in the Globe and Mail of November 27, 1989, this minister stated: "Canadian farmers are going to have to realize that farming is a business, so we are going to have to be flexible, we are going to have to adapt to the globalization, the liberalization of trade".
I think that is a very important observation because it is the reality of the situation. The world is changing out there. New trading patterns are developing and political revolutions are ongoing.
The European Community, for example, has increased its yield in grain and oilseeds by 100 per cent since the 1950s and the 1960s, at which time it was the largest importer of grain. Today it is the third largest exporter.
It is also interesting to note that Japan has become Canada's top grain buyer. The United States has become our most important customer for agricultural products including grain. In 1986 our exports of grain and oilseeds to the United States was $388 million versus $514 million. In terms of tonnes, 1,175,000 tonnes in 1986; 1,733,600 tonnes in 1988. There are markets of which we must take advantage.
This is why it is incumbent upon us to review our agricultural policies and programs. We have put our agricultural programs and policies to the supreme test with the turbulent years we have just gone through. It is important and it is wise to evaluate them.
We see the changing political landscape, particularly in the eastern European countries. We see changing trading patterns. We see changing demands and consumer habits. We see the enhancement of further technology. We a see new emphasis on food safety and on environmental considerations. It is only natural that we have to evaluate our programs.
We do so with the approach of offering hope and optimism for the future and eager to tackle the challenges of change. One thing is a constant about agriculture: change has been constant from day one. We have been successful as an agricultural community because we have been able to adapt to change.
If we are to maintain our leadership and our leading edge in the agriculture communities of the world, we must adapt to change. We must be more responsive to consumer needs. We must be more market oriented. We must take advantage of the changing trade environment. We must take advantage of the changing political scene. It is for these reasons that we must seek to devise the best programs and policies in consultation with the agriculture community, with consumers and with everyone in the food chain to engage in the most comprehensive review that has ever been embarked upon by this government.
This initiative speaks to the future, not to the past. It speaks to opportunity and success, not to failure. It is about building confidence. It is about providing the appropriate tools. It is about leadership. It is about vision and it is about new direction. It is about talking about our strengths. It is about taking stock of what we have and what we need. It is about building for the future and building an agricultural industry that is sound, that is viable, that is durable.
I invite all hon. members to assist in that challenge because to ciy gloom and doom without offering anything positive or constructive is not the way farmers will respond to the reality of the situation. Farmers will tackle the challenge and will turn that challenge into an opportunity. That is what we are talking about here. Let us not turn the clock back; let us turn it ahead. We give you the opportunity to participate in that process.

Mr. Speaker, I have some comments I want to make at this point. First of all I would like to put into correct context a statement he attributed to a former Prime Minister.


"Why should I sell your wheat?", is not the whole statement that was made. He said: "Why should I sell your wheat? You already have two government agencies selling your wheat for you. I couldn't sell it if I wanted to. I do not have the jurisdiction to do that."
The jurisdiction was with the Canadian Wheat Board and the other government marketing agencies.
I must also take the minister to task a bit because he indicated that farm income was up. Does that farm income include, for example, the off-farm income that is so essential to the effective operation of a farm today when the farmer himself and probably his wife have to go out and take a job?
I would also like to draw to his attention that it was in the last quarter of 1984 that grain prices dropped dramatically. Consequently it was under his administration. Certainly there should have been some compensation to producers when this happened.
I would also like to point out that there were droughts in 1985, 1987 and 1988 in many areas of Canada. As a result of those droughts as much as anything, a lot of farmers find themselves in difficult financial situations.
I had a phone call from one farmer from Saskatchewan just last week. The minister talks about the great policies of the government. I want to just to draw to the attention of the House one of those policies. Under this policy- and I believe it must have been a commodity based loan-a farmer had taken out a mortgage a few years ago. He has made 65 consecutive monthly payments on that mortgage and never missed one. Now his principal is actually more than it was at the start.
That is the kind of program we have had from this government and that is why that program was discontinued last summer.
A neighbour came to me in frustration last winter because it was suggested to him by the Farm Credit Corporation that he should take out a commodity based loan. By running all the figures through his computer, going back to 1972, using monthly records of prices of grain, corn, wheat and soybeans, and forecasting to the year 2008, he found it simply would not work. This is the type of program we have seen.
I am very disappointed. I have asked on a couple of occasions for a directive from the Farm Credit Corpora-

tion to the government in order that we could have a look at it. I was assured by the chairman of the Farm Credit Corporation back in late September or early October that I would get it, but I have not received it.
When I look at page 5 of the corporate plan, I read: "The acquisition of properties is expected to increase over the next three years". It goes on: "The inventory of real properties will increase dramatically over the short term". Still further I read: "Collections, recovery actions, debt review actions, debt review process, property management and marketing will continue to exceed the available staff".
This is not quite the same glowing picture that we heard about just a few minutes ago. In fact there were more properties on hand at the time the annual report was tabled than there were actual loans made last year. If the 702 staff members of the Farm Credit Corporation each made two loans a year, it would have been the total that was actually made under the Farm Credit Corporation.
There are actually more properties on hand, and I am very disturbed that this sort of thing would happen. When we look at the Farm Credit Corporation Act, Section ll(l)(e) states that it is intended that concessions and moratoriums or rewriting of mortgages, compositions, schemes, and arrangements can be made under the objects and powers of the act. It states that the corporation may do these various things. Consequently, that is the responsibility of the government in power when we come through three years of drought and difficult times and particularly the low prices that occurred shortly after it came to office. I am sure it must have been the steady hand of the previous Minister of Agriculture, the tiller of the agricultural sector, that kept things up where they were. Immediately this government came to power, look what happened. Everything started to fall apart.
There are also some other things that I am very concerned about. We talk about the restructured cases that come through the Farm Debt Review Board's reports. I think there are some 2,000. How many of these cases have actually been restructured? What is the average land base by province left owned by the farmer in these cases? Are they actually viable units, or have farmers been stripped of their land base and of their assets? Can they make a living on these farms?

We estimate that perhaps as many as 15 per cent or 20 per cent of cases are not getting restructured type concessions. We believe that the land base being left to these people is very, very small. What we have is the Farm Credit Corporation recycling these concessions back into its own corporation.

I would call on the government today to take positive steps, to look at the hardships being created across this nation, and to step in with even more funding at the present time to make the agricultural industry an economic industry with a standard of living commensurate with that of the rest of society, rather than having to face the hardships that are being forced on the people today.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member made representations more than asked questions, but I will comment on the reference that he made to the Farm Credit Corporation properties on hand.
This is a direct result of the Farm Credit Corporation sitting down with the farmer and working out an arrangement where he could stay on the land and re-establish himself. He is taking issue with that, and I suppose by taking issue with it he is suggesting that we should unload this property at fire sale prices and kick the farmers off the land. Maybe that is the policy of the Liberal party. It is certainly not our policy.
We have tried with the help of the Farm Debt Review Board to work with farmers to provide extreme latitude and accommodation through the farm debt review process, properly funded. I think the losses that the Farm Credit Corporation has endured as a result of the high interest rate policy of the former government of which he was a member was something in the order of $1.3 billion. That is what happens when you let interest rates go to 23 and 24 per cent and let inflation go to 13 and 14 per cent.
What really strikes me rather funny is that they would want us to do the same thing again. We know that there are inflationary problems in this country. We are trying to deal with that as best we can, in a balanced way. When I hear the representations across the way, if we followed
their advice we would end up in the same situation as we did in the 1981-82 period when we saw those soaring interest rates.
The reason the Farm Credit Corporation has land and inventory is that it worked out lease arrangements and other arrangements with the producers who have found themselves in difficulty. There has been an attempt to keep them there, to accommodate them, and to work with them during this very difficult period.

Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister made quite a few comments with respect to how much his government has done for agriculture. Despite that, there is no doubt that there is a lot of concern in rural Canada over the future of agriculture.
I would like to ask the minister a question with respect to transportation. As the minister will know, there is about to be or will be soon some rationalization on rail lines. That is a nice word for saying abandonment.
Some studies have been done with respect to rail abandonments. Certainly in my own riding there is a rail line known as the Central Butte branch line subdivision which was studied by the senior grain transportation committee. The result of that study recommended not to have it abandoned nor to have it retained. The committee indicated that it was a marginal line and perhaps, if it had more goods carried on that line, it would become more viable.
As the minister will be aware there are some major irrigation projects taking place on the South Saskatchewan River near Riverhurst, which presumably is going to increase production in that area. There are some farmers, as the minister indicated, who are taking the initiative. They are attempting to take the opportunity to create some more wealth and jobs in that area. They want to create an alfalfa plant. They have looked at investors, conducted studies and produced reports. However one of their concerns is the future of the rail line in that area. If the rail line is gone then the alfalfa plant is going to be no good. Their concern is the future of that line.
These people have gone to a lot of work. There are two spokespersons for them: Gordon Kent who is an agricultural engineer and Art Heshey who is a consultant for Heshey Management. As spokespeople for the Riverhurst Water Users Association they are prepared to spend their own money to come to Ottawa to put their case before the minister. If the minister will find some time to meet with them, whether it be a half hour or an
November 29, 1989

hour sometime before Christmas or at any other time, they would certainly be glad to meet him.
These farmers in Saskatchewan are trying to take agriculture in a new direction. If the minister will have time to hear them, I would certainly assist his office in helping to arrange this appointment and this meeting. Perhaps the minister could find the time in the near future.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, the issue of branch lines is one that has always been very sensitive and has involved a lot of emotion.
At the same time because of the way the freight rate structure is applied now, because of the fact that many of the branch lines are the most expensive lines to operate in terms of cost benefit, and because the costs of those lines under the new freight rate formula apply to the total system for which all farmers end up having to pay, we endeavour to try to find the most efficient transportation system available for that purpose.
As a result we have used off-line elevator systems where you build a new elevator facility and the grain is trucked. That has reduced the costs rather substantially. There are short line operations, one of which is operating in the province of Alberta and has reduced line operating costs.
I am not totally familiar with the subdivision the hon. member refers to. It is called the Central Butte subdivision. I certainly would be pleased to make representations to the Minister of Transport. As he knows, this falls within the domain of the Minister of Transport. I would be pleased to make representations to him and also attempt to see whether we could arrange a suitable time for his people to meet with him. I think if he were to meet with the Minister of Transport it would probably be very useful. I would try to arrange that.
If I cannot arrange it I would be pleased to meet with him. Perhaps his office wants to contact my office. Hopefully, we could arrange a suitable time and place for that to occur. It may not even be necessary for them to come to Ottawa. Perhaps I could meet them in western Canada, but the hon. member is certainly free to

contact my office. I would be glad to accommodate in any way I can.

Mr. Speaker, despite the programs and the statements made by the minister with respect to agriculture in this country, I think it is very fair to say that it is clearly in serious difficulty.
To see that one need only look at figures from Statistics Canada. The number of farms in Canada is now well below 300,000, down significantly from even 10 years ago. Average sales for a Canadian farm in 1986 were some $71,000 while expenses were some $60,000. Over the past three years that $11,000 gap has in fact narrowed.
It is not surprising that the number of days worked off the farm continues to increase all the time from 148 in 1960 to 173 in 1985. The fact that there are fewer farmers with less money to spend means more pressure is placed on businesses and services in rural communities, which in turn results in a rural infrastructure that indeed is very fragile.
What is this government doing to reverse this unfortunate trend? When it comes to rhetoric the government is very good. In fact, it should receive an A-plus. The tragic fact is that that is all there is: rhetoric.
While the Progressive Conservatives espouse viable family farms, in practice they are promoting huge, corporate and industrial farms.
This lack of concern for the family farm is clear when one looks at some of the policies and programs the government has implemented.
The removal of oats from the Canadian Wheat Board proved to western Canadians that although the government may claim to consult with interested groups, it simply does not. The government said that it did extensive consultation with Canadians before removing oats. When asked in the House the Minister of Agriculture had the nerve to state that he had consulted with such groups as the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission, various hog marketing boards, and various cattlemen's associations. These groups obviously had nothing to do with the production of oats. They did have one thing in

Supply
common; they happened to agree with the government's position on the oats issue.
What the minister failed to say was that the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool all opposed the government's removal of oats. As well a Decima poll, which is the same company that does polling for the Conservative party, concluded that two-thirds of farmers in western Canada wanted oats to remain under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board and three-quarters of farmers felt that they simply had not been consulted by the PC government.
Another group that was consulted, a group that the minister and others of his government are not apt to mention when discussing issues such as this one, was the international grain companies: Cargill, Continental and Elders. While the government sought no advice from the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, the advisory committee or others directly involved with the farm issue and actually growing oats in this country, it saw fit to consult with international grain traders. These companies have about as much concern for the future of family farms as does Burger King for the continued success of McDonald's.
A second program is the cash advance program. The idea behind the cash advance program was to help the family farmer receive an interest-free advance on his crop before he had an opportunity to take it to market. The government not only added an interest component to this program but increased the maximum amount that could be borrowed to $250,000.
Speaking on behalf of grain farmers from western Canada, one must either have an extremely good crop or have an awfully large farm in order to be able to borrow the $250,000 allowed under this program. The only advantage under this new program is to the very large farming operations.
I would ask this government to provide a list of those groups that have traditionally participated in this program and that support this change. Perhaps it consulted its traditional list, which includes the Canola growers, the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission, the Hog Marketing Boards and the Cattlemen's Association.
Another program that has been put on the block is the At and East program. This is a program that impacts directly on the maritimes. At and East is a program that encourages grain and flour to be exported from the ports of Halifax and St. John. If that program is cut, it is certain that the grain facilities at St. John will close and very much jeopardize those grain facilities at Halifax. It will also put an increased pressure on Dover Flour Mills, the only flour mill in the maritimes.
The loss of the program which subsidizes grain and flour movement to those ports will be a major blow to both these communities. In Halifax, the city will lose annual income of some $16 million and several hundred employees will be laid off or have their hours drastically cut. These would include, train crews, longshoremen, stevedores and maintenance workers. It is something which Halifax can ill afford.
I am informed by Dover Mills that it will be completely and effectively moved from the private flour export market and will simply have to rely on government groups like CIDA for its export markets. Since the cost of transporting the flour will increase, and since these agencies are on a fixed budget, they will actually purchase less flour, which will hurt not only Dover Flour Mills but other mills throughout the country which produce this flour.
The port of St. John will lose some $8.5 million that presently flows into its economy and hundreds of workers will be affected. This is all because the government refused to listen to the Atlantic Transportation Committee which some four years ago proposed a new format for the At and East program that would save the government at least half the cost of that program.
This government, the government that consults with Canadians to promote a better Canadian society, refused to even consider the proposal put forth by the Atlantic Transportation Committee. Instead it simply cut the program.
It is the same government that refused to listen to the advisory committee of the Canadian Wheat Board, to the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, and to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture when considering whether or not to remove oats from the Canadian Wheat Board.
Instead it chose to consult with groups such as the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission. It is the same government that has cut this program. I wonder if it

consulted with the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission when it was deciding what to do with the At and East program, because it certainly paid no attention to the Atlantic Transportation Committee.
These are crucial times for agriculture in this country. The free trade agreement and the GATT talks now being carried on are both very critical to the future of agriculture. On these talks depend the future of orderly marketing and supply management. The very foundation of agriculture in this country depends on the outcome of these talks.
Of concern to myself and of concern to many Canadian producers are the mixed signals this government is sending with respect to this crucial area. The government indicated before the election that free trade would mean greater prosperity for all Canadians including farmers. That has turned out not to be the case; certainly not yet. The opposite appears to be the case, especially for small producers.
Before the election I recall a medium-sized hog producer telling me that he was going to vote for free trade because that was his guarantee into the U.S. market. He believed that by voting for the PCs they would create a level playing field allowing him to market more easily his hogs in the U.S. There may have been a level playing field created, but I have not seen it. If there is one it certainly is a level playing field that is decidedly tipped toward the United States and decidedly tipped toward the large hog producer.
The countervail duty that has been slapped on hogs has meant that the future of that particular hog producer in my riding is in real jeopardy. One thing that I have learned since being elected is that many of the problems facing Canadians in my riding of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre also face Canadians throughout this country.
I was recently in Prince Edward Island talking to farmers in that beautiful province. The most successful farmers are often the small mixed farmers who grow a combination of those famous P.E.I. potatoes, some hay and some grain and who raise some livestock.
While I was in P.E.I. I was told that a number of mixed farmers are simply going to stop producing hogs because it simply did not pay. The reality in P.E.I. or Saskatchewan is that the only way one can successfully raise hogs is to have a large operation because the margin of profit
Supply
per hog is so small it only pays when producing them in large numbers. This is not the promise the Tories made to those people before the last election.
What of supply management? We have a system in this country that allows for a viable industry in dairy products, eggs, chickens, turkeys and broiler hatching eggs. This system ensures that Canadians control the market in these areas and ensures that fair competition continues to exist. The GATT talks that are now taking place may well force some compromise, and some altering of position in the area of supply management may be required. Certainly industries such as the dairy industry have recognized this fact and have put forth proposals in order to help their industry survive in a global market.
I am certain that there is much concern among Canadian diary producers. Certainly they have put a lot of effort into developing and bringing forth proposals. Nonetheless when they look at how much the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board and the Atlantic Transportation Committee were ignored when they offered their expert advice in their particular area, what are the chances that the dairy commission is going to have any influence on the government's position on supply management? That is, of course, unless it happens to concur with its thinking.
There is certainly room to manoeuvre in these talks. Agricultural economists make it very clear that we do not have to turn to unbridled capitalism, that it is quite possible to have an effective and efficient trading of agricultural commodities while at the same time allowing individual governments to develop programs which will allow them to maintain viable, profitable and productive family farming units. The question is whether or not this government desires to reach that very worth-while objective.
The history of this government would indicate that concern over healthy, viable family farms and a viable rural economy is simply not part of this, its consideration. The government recently released its green paper on agriculture entitled Growing Together. It is a document that is filled with platitudes on the future of agriculture in this country. If there is one thing that Canadians have learned from the government over the past five years, it

November 29, 1989
Supply
is not to trust and not too put too much faith in PC promises.
I do not want to be mistaken with respect to this document. It is welcomed because it provides Canadians with a vehicle by which to discuss the future of agriculture in this country. A proper, full and effective dialogue would allow input from all sectors of the country that have an interest in agriculture, with the final result being new policy directions which represent the views, the desires and the needs of all Canadian producers, not just the large corporate conglomerates but all Canadians, from the potato farmer in Prince Edward Island to the apple grower in British Columbia.
I want to believe that the PCs are serious with this consultative process. I want to believe that they have the genuine interests of all Canadian producers at heart. I want to believe it but I am, unfortunately, simply skeptical. I am skeptical because when I look at the past record of this government, I see that that simply has not been the case.
Before I close, I want to focus on one more subject, policies for agriculture, we must remember that it is only part of the over-all world economy.
Today the rural infrastructure of this country is in tatters, whether it be in Nova Scotia, Quebec, Ontario, Saskatchewan or British Columbia. The economic base of many communities is disappearing. Small businesses are closing their doors and services are simply being lost. The result is that seniors are leaving, not because they want to but rather because they are forced to. At the same time, young families are reluctant to move into these smaller centres, not only because of the scarce employment but also because of the fact that there is a lack of not only amenities but essential services as well.
Here again, the government must accept responsibility for the programs that exist in this area. There are many programs that are being cut and there are many problems that are being created.
The removal of VIA Rail takes away a necessary lifeline to many communities. What is even more disheartening is that this government is about to embark on a wholesale removal of track from large areas of this country. We all know that once the railway is gone, the death-knell is rung for many of these communities. While this may prove to be of benefit to Canadian
Pacific, it certainly will not be of benefit to large areas of rural Canada.
As well, this government has a blind determination to eliminate hundreds of postal offices in this country, thereby putting a greater strain on rural communities. These are not just closures of post offices that have 50 and 75 boxes, the government is closing post offices in large communities of 2,000 to 3,000 people. This means that people in those communities, which are of a relatively stable size, are not going to be able to receive the same mail service that millions of other Canadians simply take for granted.
In closing, I would like to say that a vital and a vibrant rural Canada provides this country with a dimension that we simply cannot afford to lose. It is possible to have healthy family farms operating in a strong rural environment. It is possible if this government has the commitment. We in the New Democratic Party are willing to work toward that end. But the question is, is the Conservative Party? Looking at its past record, I would say that it is not. Our challenge in this party is to try to teach an old dog a new trick, and that trick would be one of compassion, concern and commitment to viable family farms in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to take part in the debate this afternoon. I must say, however, that I am a little disappointed in the direction that the debate has taken because, quite frankly, the rhetoric flies in the face of the record.
The Minister of Agriculture has stated quite clearly in his earlier presentation the significance of the amount of funding that has been given by this government to agriculture and I am not going to take time at this point to review the significant increases in support to farmers put forward by this government in comparison with that put forward by previous administrations.
I think the government is very clear also in stating that the family farm is the essence of agriculture in Canada. Ninety-nine per cent of all the farms in this countiy are owned by farm families. Ninety-six per cent of the total production of agriculture in this countiy comes from family farms.
November 29, 1989

I think it is very significant that our support includes things like the dairy support policy, tripartite stabilization, all the various agricultural stabilization programs, drought support, crop insurance, and on we go through the great array of programs for Canadian agriculture, and each one of them put in place for the expressed reason of supporting family farms in Canada.
Looking at programs for the future, the document that the minister put forward just a week ago entitled Growing Together again is an indication of the significance of farm families to the future of this industry and the importance that the government places on those people. It clearly indicates the level of consultation that will go on in the future as we look for improvements in our agricultural policies.
I want to very briefly look at the direction of agricultural policy, particularly relating to trade. I think it is safe to say that this motion is brought forward today really to cover the disorganization which occurs in the opposition parties.
I would invite anyone to look closely at the presentations made by opposition speakers today, and look for positive alternatives that are being put forward in those presentations. I am sure that observers will find very few. It will be a continual carping and complaining about what is going on in the industry of agriculture today, but I can almost be assured that there will be very few positive alternatives put forward.
I think it is important to look at some of the accusations that are being made and see what the other side of the story is from what we may be hearing in the House today from various other people. The minister has stated that trade accounts for about 50 per cent of agricultural revenues. Clearly, this is very significant to our farmers and to the over-all economy of Canada.
We want to liberalize trade but we also want to protect important features in our agricultural system. One of those important features, of course, is supply management. Our critics will say that we have not supported supply management with enough vigour in recent discussions with the United States and particularly in international negotiations under GATT. I think the evidence flies in the face of the comments that are being made here today.
Supply
I would like to review a few of the statements put forward by spokespeople for the agricultural industry and in particular leaders of the various supply management sectors. I refer first of all to a press release put out by the dairy farmers of Canada in which there are statements by John Killoran, the president of the Dairy Farmers of Canada, who states, referring to the GATT panel ruling:
"The ruling clearly illustrates the inability of the current GATT
wording to safeguard effective supply management programs."
When the Minister of Agriculture formed the dairy task force, Mr. Killoran stated that they welcomed the opportunity to be involved in consultations with the Minister of Agriculture as well as officials of External Affairs regarding the strategy the Canadian Government should pursue in future negotiations.
Clearly the leaders of the supply management sector are involved in the discussions, they are meeting regularly with the Canadian negotiators and it is obvious from their press release that they are pleased with that involvement and that level of consultation.
In a report of October 27 in The Globe and Mail, Nelson Coyle, a spokesman for the Canadian Chicken Marketing Agency, refers to their opportunities to talk with Michael Gifford and he states that he is pleased with the stance of Michael Gifford, the Canadian agricultural negotiator, when they did not endorse various parts of the U.S. trade initiatives and their position at GATT. Again, the area which Canada did not endorse was the area which restricted imports, and of course, that is so important to protecting our supply management systems here in Canada.
A third reference relates to an open letter by Mr. Bill Mitchell, assistant director for the Ontario Milk Marketing Board, who comments on the ice cream and yoghurt situation:
There is nothing fair about the U.S. move and the Canadian
government has taken a strong stand against it.
Those are entirely different comments from the ones we have heard from the opposition critics today. It is clear that the government is very much in support of organized marketing in this country where it has become so much a part of the Canadian industry.
Today in the House the Minister for International Trade commented on the position that was reached and

recently taken in Bangkok, again in favour of supply management in the particular sectors where it applies.
I would like to refer again to a spokesman from Australia, a person who is outside Canada, outside whatever internal arguments and discussions that may be going on here relating to various trade initiatives. The article said that the Canadian delegation found itself under some criticism when the Australian trade minister, Michael Duffy, told local journalists that Canada's insistence on maintaining protection for its dairy industry could be a problem in reaching a final consensus.
Those are hardly the words that we are hearing here today, but out of that meeting, there was an agreement. Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the motion moved by the Hon. Member for Algoma, a motion that is very negative about agriculture in this country.
In his preamble, the hon. member mentioned the farmers, mostly from Quebec and Ontario, who visited Ottawa last week, but he failed to mention the reasons behind their visit. If he had bothered to listen, he would have realized that our farmers came to ask us to protect their vested interests. Although the situation is not ideal, they know perfectly well they are protected by all kinds of measures put in place by the government, and they came to see us to make sure these measures would not be jeopardized by the current negotiations.
I will try to give en overview of the situation, and I think we will see it is not as dramatic and certainly more positive than the motion presented by the hon. member for Algoma would have us believe.
It is true that Canadian agriculture and the agri-food business generally have reached a turning point in their history. We will probably have to make some bold and innovative changes to be able to respond to new needs in the industry in the 90's and the 21st century.
First of all, I think I should explain the context in which such changes are being initiated. During the past five years we went through a period that in some ways was worse than the Depression. As a result of high interest rates at the beginning of this decade and poorly designed financing programs, we had many major problems which only now are beginning to subside.
The economy does of course have an impact, but to answer the Opposition's motion condemning this government, I think we should look at things in their proper perspective. Today, we are still suffering the consequences of the lack of foresight and economic vision that was typical of the beginning of this decade.
Mr. Speaker, our colleagues opposite are trying to play their role as the Opposition in this House, but perhaps they should first examine their own consciences.
We have to go back to the 70's and the then spiralling price of land to get to the root of the financing problems that ensued. People who bought land when prices reached all-time highs put themselves in a very vulnerable situation.
We received a legacy of loans with low collaterals and hign interest rates and land values that were going down. Low prices for farm products, the result of a number of complex economic factors, have led to major arrears in debt payments by farmers, to foreclosures, bankruptcies and a crisis of confidence in the industry.
Obviously, the droughts we experienced and the merciless trade war between the Americans and the European Economic Community have added to the many difficulties we already had.
November 29, 1989

That being said, we are pleased to note that the number of bankruptcies has declined since 1985, from 353 to 220 in 1988. This trend has continued in the first eight months of 1989 in Canada with another 2 per cent average decrease compared to the same period in 1988. The worst is over and we are at last beginning to see signs of improvement.
Not only is farm debt going down, but so is the amount of overdue debt. Moreover, interest charges are expected to account for 13 per cent of total operating expenses in 1989, which is 19 per cent less than in 1981 and hardly more than they were in the 1970s. Although interest rates have increased over the last year, it must be borne in mind that they only add slightly less than 2 per cent to farmers' operating costs.
The average farm family income is now nearly at the same level as that of other Canadian families. Family farms are all in all in pretty good shape at the end of the 1980s. In 1987, the average Canadian farmer had an 80 per cent equity, worth a sizable $373,000, in his farm. Average income, including off-farm earnings, was around $36,000. Furthermore, new farmers are waiting to take over and young people are still going into farming.
Before overcoming these difficulties, we learned some important lessons. We must now act on the basis of past experience and we are already well on the way. We must adjust to change if we want to remain competitive in a constantly changing, increasingly global market. That is why our government has adopted long-term planning. We are now reviewing all of our agricultural policies and programs to make them more effective and to adapt them to the issues facing us.
Obviously, farm finances are a key element in building a more competitive agri-food industry and they are therefore an important part of the review. Nevertheless, farm finances must not be limited to credit issues alone. They also involve the management and financing of agricultural enterprises, which are part of the larger farm income protection system.
Given the wrong ideas concerning the vitality of this industry, it is not surprising that opinions are so divided on setting a long-term financial policy for this sector. For example, are subsidized interest rates the solution to most farmers' financial problems or on the contrary, as
Supply
some groups claim, are they not rather an incentive to excessive debt?
We know that extending credit in itself is not enough. As we look to the future, our goal must be to meet financial needs as we help farmers manage risks and avoid major financial problems.
Mr. Speaker, we do not claim to have solved all problems. The situation remains difficult in some sectors, particularly grains and oil seeds, as well as pork production. Some family farms still have trouble paying off their debt.
Nevertheless, the Government has made remarkable efforts in the past five years to rectify the situation. I can assure all hon. members of this House that this government will continue to give farmers all the help required for their farms to remain profitable and prosperous, even in the context of the objectives of responsible financial management it has set itself.
Mr. Speaker, you are indicating to me that I must conclude. We must deal with all these issues and more to help farmers prepare properly for the 1990s. As you can see, the present government cannot be blamed for farmers' problems. On the contrary, we are convinced that considerable efforts have been made to correct the situation and mechanisms are in place so that we can adjust rapidly to the new challenges presented by the globalization of markets, which has already begun.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the latitude, given the limited time available for the remaining members to make some comments.
I would like to reflect upon the previous speaker's comments regarding the government initiatives in agriculture. We on this side tend to think of them as being a lack of initiatives.
Certainly this concept of trying to create a level playing field is just simply unworkable in the light of the reality of Canadian agriculture. The fact is that we suffer significant disadvantages in Canada as a result of our shorter growing season, our lower levels of production because of the economy of scale, our greater transporta-

November 29, 1989
Supply
tion costs, our higher construction costs and, of course, higher energy costs because of our competitors to the south. So it is impossible to create this level playing field as the members on the government side seem wont to do. In fact, we feel that maintaining a viable agricultural industry in Canada is going to require some considerable and continued government input.
As a matter of fact, I would remind the House that the Macdonald Commission, when it tabled its extensive report, recommended that agriculture be excluded from the free trade agreement that we have now signed and in which we are involved. Although the commission recommended against it, this government has gone into a free trade agreement in agricultural commodities and the U.S. has won major concessions such as the reduction of the powers of the Wheat Board, the removal of transportation subsidies, and the eventual phase-out of agricultural tariffs. If that is not a capitulation to U.S. demands, I do not know what is. As a result of this, the whole concept of supply management and marketing boards and the stability that those boards give the agricultural industry in Canada is in fact severely jeopardized.
As a matter of fact, Article 703 of the free trade agreement that we have now signed, talks about market access for agriculture and states that in order to facilitate trade in agricultural goods, the parties, meaning Canada and the United States, shall work together to improve access to each other's market through the elimination and reduction of import barriers. That means those kinds of price structuring systems such as the marketing boards and the supply management boards that have come to be the stability of the industry. When they are gone, it is going to be very, very difficult for agriculturalists right across Canada to compete.
When referring to the free trade agreement, the American Farm Bureau concluded that once tariffs were removed, American grains, bakery goods, poultry, eggs and milk products would gain greater access to the Canadian market and undermine the power of marketing boards. In Western Perspectives an article written in April of 1988, there was actually a comment by the minister, and the minister himself had identified significant losses in jobs in British Columbia agriculture as a
result of the implementation of that free trade agreement, as much as admitting that agriculture is going to take it on the chin as a result of the FTA.
The Okanagan and Shuswap area in British Columbia, with an agricultural industry that is concentrated in soft fruits, becomes virtually a region of sacrifice under this free trade agreement. It is going to be very, very difficult for those farmers to compete once those tariff structures come down.
I have talked with farmers in the Okanagan, grape growers who over the last year have tom out their vines. I have asked them what they are going to do with their land, what they are going to plant on that land. Their response is: "I am going to try to sell the land because no matter what I plant I am not going to be able to make it. It is as simple as that."
We are talking about the demise of an industry. It is beyond me to listen to the rhetoric that this government is giving from the other side of the House on how vibrant our agricultural industry is. Good heavens, if it was so vibrant, why did we have 7,000 farmers on the front lawn of the House of Commons here last week demanding some action by this minister because of the very, very deep concern that they have about the future of the agricultural industry in Canada?
I speak for the farmers throughout the Okanagan, throughout British Columbia, but more so for the farmers from the west coast to the east coast. We have a serious problem in terms of the future of our agricultural industry in Canada. We cannot compete on the concept of a level playing field simply because of the inequities in the geographic and climatic factors that face agriculture in this land. We have to recognize that and we have to protect it.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by congratulating the hon. member for Algoma and the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex, who today presented this motion of censure in the House, a motion that reads as follows:

That this House condemn the government for its insensitivity to the tremendous difficulties being faced by Canada's farmers and other rural Canadians-
Mr. Speaker, I believe Canadian agriculture is in a precarious state. On November 21, here on Parliament Hill, we saw one of the biggest demonstrations of discontent in the agricultural sector in the past ten years. Mr. Speaker, I believe that the only farmers' protest that may have been bigger than the one on November 21 was in 1973-74, when milk producers were demanding better ways of adjusting to the new supply management system, a system that today, those same farmers want to protect.
What is behind these demonstrations? Mr. Speaker, farmers are demonstrating because they are worried about the positions that are being taken, and the ones that are not being taken, by the present government at the GATT talks now being held. As you know, GATT Article 11 is threatened by positions being taken by many countries, including the Cairns Group and the United States. These countries want to weaken or repeal altogether the GATT measures that allow us here in Canada to have supply management systems.
Mr. Speaker, in recent months we saw that the United States had every intention of preventing us, and even appealed to GATT to prevent Canada from imposing quantitative restrictions on imports of ice cream and yogurt. Ironically, Mr. Speaker, the United States, thanks to a special GATT article, is exempt from the same measures it would impose on us. In other words, the United States wants to be able to export its yogurt and ice cream to Canada, while being able to invoke measures that would prevent exports of yogurt and ice cream from Canada to the United States. Of course, Canada does not, at this very moment, intend to export yogurt and ice cream to the United States, but the fact remains that there is a double standard here.
The consultation document provided by the Minister of Agriculture has also disturbed many farmers in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. This document challenges our transport system, marketing and many support programs in Canada's agricultural industry. In fact, we could even say that, to a certain extent, this report threatens the very existence of our supply management systems.
Supply
The case of crop advance payments is another example of the careless attitude of this Conservative government towards Canada's farming community. Crop insurance reductions are yet another example. And, finally so is farm credit. We all know that the Farm Credit Corporation's current interest rate stands at about 13 per cent, which is nearly 9 per cent over and above the inflation rate in this country. I think we can safely say it has to be the highest rate ever in the history of the FCC, if we take into account the real interest rate.
It peaked at over 20 per cent in the past!

I see some members across the aisle who do not agree with me. I would urge them to take a closer look at the file and, like me, they will realize I am telling the truth.
Mr. Speaker, I have here a table released by Statistics Canada which indicates, among other things, that in 1977 the prime rate and the Consumer Price Index were 8.5 and 7.9 per cent respectively, which means that the actual loan rate was then less than 1 per cent.
Referring to 1982- I see that a member opposite is talking about 1982 when the prime rate stood at 15 per cent and the CPI at 10.8 per cent. The real rate of interest therefore was 5 per cent. Now, in the fall of 1989, the CPI is under 5 per cent and, as I pointed out earlier, the prime rate is 13.5 per cent. We can see that the real interest rate right now is very high, I would even say it is undoubtedly the highest we have had in the past 10 years, notwithstanding the fact that we are neither in an economic recession nor in particularly trying times in terms of the over-all economy. I strongly urge, therefore, the Tory Members opposite to pressure the Minister of Finance into greatly reducing this interest rate.
How time flies, Mr. Speaker! There are a great many other issues I wish I could bring to the attention of my hon. colleagues. To conclude, I should like to emphasize the fact that the Tory government, in its last budget, inflicted some severe cuts on the Canadian farm industry. Here are a few examples of these cuts: advance payments for grain and crops: $54 million; dairy product export program: $12 million; Canadian Dairy Commission: $10 million; crop insurance: $200 million; grain and flour movement: $60 million; railway track rehabilitation: $48 million; farm product loan program: $15 million. Alltogether, Mr. Speaker, $399 million were cut from the farm budget during 1989. It goes without saying that

Supply
the farmers who came to demonstrate in front of Parliament these past few days had every reason to do so. They gave us a warning. The farmers promised in front of the media and the Canadian people that if things did not change, they intended to return and that they would be 30,000, 40,000, or even 50,000 to demonstrate on Parliament Hill, and not only 7,000, 8,000 or 10,000. I know that Canadian farmers are quite able to do so. But this is not the issue. The real issue is: Should farmers have to use such methods to get their fair share of the pie? The answer is no.
The Tory Government opposite should know by now that the Canadian people want our farm industry to get assistance. We want to maintain our farm industry alive and healthy. A country which loses its farm industry will eventually lose control over its economy.

Mr. Speaker, these are serious times for rural Canada and our farmers. The insensitivity of this government to the plight of the agricultural industry is unforgivable.
To listen to this government and the part-time Minister of Agriculture here tonight, you would think that nothing was done for agriculture before this government came along. You would think that there had never been co-operation between the provinces and the federal government, or our trading partners for that matter. You would think the current programs that have built an agricultural industry that is envied the world over just happened by chance, not as an answer to problems in the agricultural sector.
The programs developed in the past by a Liberal government and, yes, by the minister's predecessor, may not have been perfect. But in a country in a northern hemisphere producing 60 per cent of its food further north than in any other nation in the world, we became the envy of other nations. We have become one of the most efficient, productive, quality-conscious agriculture producers anywhere in the world. Leaders from all across the world have indicated this to us.
Now we have a Green Paper Growing Together. The government is saying that former policies are wrong, that the Hon. John Wise was wrong and that farm income support programs must be changed, supply management reformed and farmers, in four words in that document, "are on their own". Quite frankly we have heard throughout the agricultural community, and everyone knows, that the former Minister of Agriculture, John Wise, resigned because he knew about the policies this government was going to bring in and that they would adversely affect the farmers for whom he worked so hard.
The part-time Minister of Agriculture, without ever consulting the agricultural sector, has come out with his salvation for agriculture. The report is full of rhetorical phrases like "global trade liberalization, self-reliance and self-sufficiency". Farmers who have had time to study the document have called it patronizing and insulting. They are telling farmers that from now on they are on their own. Comforting, do you not think?
The minister is now saying that he is the Messiah, that his predecessors, farm organizations and farmers do not understand the needs of agriculture, only he does.
As loudly demonstrated last week by thousands of farmers on Parliament Hill, the agricultural sector is asking why this government is throwing Canadian agriculture to the wolves. They asked: "Why are you abandoning us?"
The minister has admitted in Growing Together his willingness to abandon product lines or a sector of agriculture no longer in demand in the market. What does this mean? What happens if the market for a certain product declines this year and a decision from on high is made not to encourage or support this sector?
As most people realize, you just do not turn the agricultural sector and production on and off like a tap. Once you lose production it takes time to re-establish production. It takes time to re-establish these production lines and, if you need it in the future, you lose your historical market figures and your future markets. More important, you are now dependent on someone else to produce that product. This becomes a serious problem if you depend on another country for your food production. Is this where we are heading? I say to you, this is where
November 29, 1989

we are heading under this government and its policies on agriculture and trade.
More emphasis is to be put on marketing, yet Cana-grex was established precisely for this purpose. This government killed this agricultural export program. Frankly, this government and this minister simply reject any suggestions from anyone simply as a matter of course. They do not listen to or care about what Canadian farmers are saying. Instead, it pushes ahead blindly, cutting up programs that have made our industry strong and made our industry the envy of the world over.
Let us look briefly at what the government has done and what it is planning to do to our agricultural industry. The record has been a long line of broken promises. Before the election the agriculture and trade ministers indicated that the free trade agreement would not adversely affect agriculture, that by putting ice cream and yoghurt on the import control list there would not be any repercussions, the industry would be protected.
Now we see the reality. Now we are being harassed by the United States over these commodities. A GATT panel has ruled that the restrictions limiting the quantity of ice cream and yoghurt allowed into Canada do not conform with Canada's GATT obligations. Quite frankly, this minister should have known that. He should not have gone across this country and told Canadian farmers that their industry would be protected.
The tobacco industry, an industry of prime importance in my riding, has also been destroyed by this government. During the election campaign the Minister of Agriculture said that Ottawa wanted to send a strong message to the tobacco industry that it will support tobacco producers in their time of adjustment. Well, shortly after the election was over this government cut back on programs to support tobacco farmers moving into other sectors. Quite a promise. The government cut them back by $6 million.
The government continued its attack on the agricultural community through this budget. The Ontario Federation of Agriculture estimated that the budget will cost Canadian farmers $120 million more in fuel and gasoline taxes this fiscal year. Some farm organizations estimate the budget will cost an individual farmer up to $2,000. Even the government's own officials have said that each farmer will be paying between $700 and $1,000
Supply
more. No other sector was so hard hit in this budget, no other sector was asked to give up so much.
Cutting the interest free payments in the Advance Payments for Crops Act will cost farmers an extra $27 million. In relative terms of the whole over-all budget this is not a great amount, a small amount for the value it was worth to Canadian farmers to allow a Canadian commodity group to market their products in such a way as to get a fair return for their work.
The government will also be cutting back $200 million in the crop insurance program, saying it is rebalancing the cost. Producers suggested a one-third tripartite funding proposal which was rejected. Without an equitable funding mechanism such as this, crop insurance premium costs will remain too expensive for many growers, especially in the poorer provinces, meaning a continuation of low participation percentages among producers of many farm commodities. Without a high participation percentage the economic and political need for ad hoc disaster relief programs will continue just as it has in the past.
The dairy industry was attacked once more. The budget eliminated $7 million from the special dairy export program and $7 million is to be cut for the Canadian Dairy Commission.
Agriculture is also unfairly treated by the GST. The Minister of Finance's technical paper on the new federal sales tax says sales of farmland will generally be subject to the normal GST rules. Sales or leases of farmland will be taxable. In other words, if one farmer sells a quarter section to another, it will be subject to the 9 per cent tax. Apparently, even land leased by a son from his father will be taxed. That is criminal.
I will conclude by saying that this government's programs with regard to agriculture, its promises during the election campaign to protect agriculture from the free trade agreement and from American harassment, and its budget cuts have all been devastating to our agricultural sector and our rural communities throughout Canada.
This side of the House will not stand for this. Let me make myself clear that in the next election the Canadian people will tell this government that they reject its agricultural policies and that there will not be one single

Mr. Speaker, I would like to use this opportunity in addressing the House to again raise questions about the future of agriculture and the future of farming in western Canada.
First of all, I would like to thank my own party, and particularly the speaker before me, for helping Parliament realize the importance of this issue. As many of the members here today on the last day of this short week have listened, they have come to understand that the reality is that Canadians are gradually beginning to realize just how fragile the agriculture economy is.
I would like to use this occasion to put what is going on in western Canada in some political and historical context. One of the reasons why western Canada has been known as the country of political protest is that one political party after another has failed to respond to the needs of western Canadian farmers. The rise of the CCF and the rise of the Social Credit Party can both be attributed in part to the failure of the central government to respond to the needs of western Canadians.
Perhaps one of the most dramatic changes in western Canadian history was the rise of the Conservatives under John Diefenbaker. He symbolized the need of western Canadians to have a greater say in the government. That
tradition has been going on since the late 1950s and in fact helped propel the current government into power.
What you see taking place in western Canada right now, gradually, but nevertheless in a very real form, is the rise of the Reform Party. Just as before, people have to consider what the state is right now of the western Canadian farmer that contributes to the rise of yet another party in western Canada. The reality is the failure of the central government, the failure of Ottawa, to respond to the needs of the western farmer.
This is a particularly bitter experience for western Canadian farmers because they thought they finally had a group of people who understood their needs. Instead, what they have right now is a minister who earlier this afternoon stood up and defended the fact that they had not been able to do anything for the farmer, saying: "What else can you expect? It is so expensive. There are too many international rules. There is a regime out there that we are not able to compete with". He is not able to say anything positive. He is only able to say: "We have done everything we can".
Well, that is not acceptable for the western Canadian farmer because we are putting at risk people who have staked their whole lives, their careers, their families, their communities on the success of their annual operations. We cannot stand by and simply say: "Well, we tried hard, but there is nothing we can do about it".
Our party, to its credit, has continually asked the House to increase activities on behalf of the Canadian farmer, particularly the western Canadian farmer. We have made proposals on financing farms, we have made proposals on GATT, we have made proposals under the free trade agreement. We have been the party of ideas. We have been the party that-

You do not want to recognize it, because you had to listen to your minister and you are embarrassed. I do not blame you. Nevertheless, the reality is the Canadian farmer is not being served by this government.
In rural Canada right now there is an added complexity on which this government is very silent, and that is the future of the very communities that are there to serve the farmer. Communities as big as Winnipeg or as tiny as Carmen or some other small communities in the Interlake area of Manitoba are all at risk, in part because of the failure of the family farm to be maintained and to be

assisted by the federal government whether in marketing, finance, research or whatever.
This reality causes a tremendous anxiety among young people. At one time we used to boast that our biggest export was grain. Right now, as members on this side realize, the biggest export out of western Canada is young people. In fact, the Saskatchewan government has a clock ticking which shows how many people leave every hour. You can imagine what it does to a province to talk not about how it is contributing to the Gross National Product every hour but how it is losing people by the hour.
Similarly in Winnipeg our population has changed very significantly in the last 15 years because people do not see a future there, in part because of the decline of the agricultural sector.
Several people have come forward and asked the government to respond to what they call this frontier cancer; several associations and several small towns. It is interesting to note that even though the Minister of Agriculture stands up and talks about his own department, he never really addresses the question of what they are doing in the job creation branch of the Department of Employment.
What are they doing in the department of the Secretary of State to help small associations? What are they doing across the board to make sure that people realize that there is a life for them in small towns in Canada; that there is a communication system for them; that the road system, through federal-provincial agreements, will be maintained; that their education system will be maintained; that there is distance education for example? All these things are lacking in the approach of the federal government.
I suppose that one could argue that the Minister of Agriculture does not have the strength, as Deputy Prime Minister, to convince his colleagues, but I think there are other ministers who from time to time come out of the west who visit these communities and they should be able to reflect the interests of westerners in the national process.
I think that perhaps Parliament should take the opportunity to take a non-partisan approach to the problems of western farmers, that we should not be satisfied with Opposition Day debates, with unresponsive legislation, with a committee system that does not respond to their needs and international negotiating

teams that do not quite understand what is going on in western Canada.
I think this is an opportunity for us to come together in an all-party sense, to join in and support resolutions such as this which, for once, says: "All right, we are making mistakes, we aren't doing enough, we've got to show some symbolic support".
Too often the western Canadian farmer picks up a newspaper and finds out the opposition is howling and the government is unresponsive. They become so cynical about this process that they turn around and go for yet another political party because they think that Parliament, as it is now structured, cannot respond. Why do you think that the concept of an elected Senate is so popular in the west? They want an elected Senate because they do not feel that the House of Commons can respond to them.
We are a land of producers, not just of people, and the Canadian system punishes producers because they do not have the support in the House of Commons. It is time that those people in the more populous areas turn to the west and understand, as consumers, that it is to the interest of everyone in this country to ensure the success of the western Canadian farmer. We cannot turn around and say that that is enough.
In keeping with the good will of the House I will do as you asked and stop early to allow the opposition to say a few words. I am sure we will hear everything they have to say in the next 30 seconds.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the House would agree to give two or three minutes to the hon. member.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to the last speaker, we are the government, that is the opposition.
I am prompted to rise by the remarks of the hon. member from Haldimand-Norfolk. Every time he rises in this House he condemns our federal Minister of Agriculture, a man who has devoted most of his time to that portfolio. If he had been in the House earlier today and listened to what that hon. gentleman had said-

I was in the House.

Supply

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
You should have listened when you were sitting there. Then you would know what this party and this government has done for agriculture in this country. Take heart and listen to it because it is something that is very, very good for all of us.
You talk about our Green Paper. What are we doing? Almost every day there are articles in the newspapers. Here is one which states: "Fed report welcome". You condemn that action as well.
There is another which states: "Canadian chicken and egg spokesmen are upbeat about Agriculture Minister Don Mazankowski's report on the future of agriculture".
"I find the paper to be extremely encouraging," said Ontario Chicken Board general manager Bill Doyle.
"You can agree with the basic thrust," said Canadian Egg Marketing Agency general manager Gerry Gartner.
I have all kinds of other ones in here.
Come on.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Okay, listen. I listened to you, you can listen to me.
I made sense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
This is from The Ottawa Citizen:
Canadian producers would be wise to fret less about GATT and
heed the wise advice of Agriculture Minister Don Mazankowski.
Marketing boards should worry less about their own quotas and
costs, he said, and more about their customers.
Another article in the paper quotes Roger Cram, general manager of the Canadian Chicken Marketing Agency in Ottawa. He said: "We reiterate our support for Mr. Mazankowski's initiative and will actively co-operate in any discussion that will lead-"

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.
With good will we offered the parliamentary secretary an opportunity to speak, and I think it would be fair for him to make his comments. However, if we need press clippings we can send for them in the mail. If he has one very final and quick remark we would be happy to hear from him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
In any event, we have talked about consultation. This minister has provided consultation with commodity groups and the provincial ministers of agriculture from across this country.
There is a policy conference to be held December 11 and 12, and the hon. member is invited to take part. Rather than sit back and complain and criticize, why not take part and grow together? The minister has offered an invitation to the people of this country to take part in forming the direction and policies of agriculture.
Mr. Speaker, I see that it is six o'clock. Thank you very much.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It being 6 p.m., it is my duty to advise the House that, pursuant to Standing Order 81(17), the proceedings on this opposition motion have expired.
